"Miscalculation of Default Period"

It is relevant to mention that our client conducted sales transactions with Midas Clothing Limited (MCL), which operates as an exporter and is registered under the Export Processing Zone Authority (EPZA). As an exporter, MCL operates outside the jurisdiction of Pakistan and is not obligated to obtain registration under section 14 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Consequently, our client claimed zero rating for supplies made to MCL, as per Serial No. 5 of the Fifth Schedule of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Furthermore, unlike Serial No. 6A of the Fifth Schedule, which previously required exporters registered under EPZA to obtain registration under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, no such condition or restriction was imposed by the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR). However, this clause was omitted through the Finance (Supplementary) Act, 2022.

In response to your queries, we provide the following detailed explanations:

2. Firstly, we wish to inform your office that MCL, being an exporter registered under the EPZA, falls outside the purview of Pakistan's jurisdiction. Additionally, as per section 14 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, MCL does not meet the criteria for mandatory registration. For clarity, the relevant section is provided below.

14. Registration.— (1) Every person engaged in making taxable supplies in Pakistan, including zero-rated supplies, in the course or furtherance of any taxable activity carried on by him, falling in any of the following categories, if not already registered, is required to be registered under this Act, namely: [List of categories]

(2) Persons not engaged in making taxable supplies in Pakistan, if required to be registered for making imports or exports, or under any provisions of the Act, or any other Federal law, may apply for registration.

3. Additionally, we draw your attention to various judgments from the Honorable High Courts and the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, where it has been established that further tax is not applicable if the buyer of goods is not required to be registered. Some notable judgments include:

• 2021 PTD 1608 LHC dated June 8, 2021 (Muhammad Arif Ice Factory)
• 2019 PTD 1858 SHC dated March 13, 2019 (Ashrafi Bread Industries)
• 2019 PTD 1958 SHC dated January 31, 2019 (Lajpal Rice Mills)
• 2018 PTD 1600 SHC dated July 14, 2017 (Zarina Glass Industries)
• 2016 PTD 648 SHC dated September 29, 2015 (Digicom Trading)
• 2015 PTD 175 LHC dated May 5, 2014 (Zia Brothers)
• 2020 PTD 1540 (Trib.) dated January 7, 2020 (Mujahid Oil Refinery)
• Tribunal's order in STA No. 197/LB/2017 dated June 1, 2017 (Diamond Tyres)

4. A pertinent judgment from the Lahore High Court, reported as 2015 PTD 175 in the case of Zia Brothers v. Federation of Pakistan, highlights the principle behind the imposition of further tax. The court emphasized that further tax aims to incentivize registration and implies a lawful obligation to obtain registration. The relevant excerpt from the judgment is provided below.

[Excerpt from the judgment]

5. Another significant case is the judgment of the Lahore High Court in the case of Muhammad Arif Ice Factory v. Federation of Pakistan (2021 PTD 1608), where the court affirmed the applicability of further tax to cases where a person is engaged in making taxable supplies but is not liable to be registered under the Act. The court's ruling underscores the interpretation of the term "liable to be registered" and its implications for the imposition of further tax.

In conclusion, we assert that MCL, as the purchaser of goods, is not required to be registered under the Act and is therefore not liable to pay further tax. We respectfully request your office to refrain from drawing any adverse inferences in this regard. Summary of CIR(A) Findings:

The Appellate Authority noted that the Appellant had fulfilled their sales tax obligations by depositing the required amount with the SRB. However, despite this compliance, the DCIR disallowed input tax deduction, citing a lack of specific documentation related to foreign services.

The Appellant's Representative (AR) emphasized the principle of consistency in tax assessments and highlighted that the sudden change in stance by the DCIR without affording the Appellant proper opportunities to be heard is unjustifiable. The AR supported their argument with relevant case laws, stressing the legal obligation for taxation officers to maintain consistency and provide fair opportunities for taxpayers to present their cases.

Additionally, the AR argued that the provisions of sections 7(2) and 23 of the Act, concerning tax invoice requirements, apply only to taxable supplies of goods, not services. Since the Appellant is a service recipient, they are not bound by these provisions. The AR also pointed out that the absence of contracts or original invoices does not automatically render input tax inadmissible, as confirmed by legal precedents.

Considering the arguments presented, the CIR(A) concluded that the AR adequately demonstrated and provided ample explanation to justify that the input tax paid and claimed relates to the Appellant's core business activity of exploration and production of oil and gas. Therefore, the onus now shifts to the department to rebut why the input tax is inadmissible considering the taxable activity of the Appellant.

In light of these findings, the CIR(A) deemed it appropriate to annul the order-in-original and directed the DCIR to re-examine the submissions of the Appellant after affording them a reasonable opportunity to be heard. If the submissions are found unsatisfactory, the DCIR is directed to pass a speaking order with proper reasoning regarding the inadmissibility of the input tax claimed by the Appellant.

Subject: Favorable Conclusion of Appeal by Commissioner (Appeals) [CIR(A)]

Dear [Client],

I am pleased to inform you that we have received a favorable decision from the Commissioner (Appeals) [CIR(A)] regarding your appeal filed against the assessment order under section 11(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The appeal pertained to the disallowance of input tax amounting to Rs 42 million on the contention that the said input tax did not pertain or relate to the taxability of the taxpayer.

After thorough consideration of the case, the CIR(A) has concluded in your favor. Below are the key findings of the CIR(A):

1. The Appellant's Representative (AR) demonstrated that the required sales tax amount was deposited with the SRB, indicating compliance with tax obligations.
2. Despite this compliance, the DCIR disallowed the input tax deduction, citing a lack of specific documentation related to foreign services.
3. The AR emphasized the principle of consistency in tax assessments and highlighted legal precedents supporting the appellant's case.
4. It was argued that provisions regarding tax invoice requirements apply only to taxable supplies of goods, not services, and the absence of certain documentation does not automatically render input tax inadmissible.
5. The CIR(A) found the AR's arguments convincing and concluded that the input tax claimed relates to the core business activity of exploration and production of oil and gas.
6. Consequently, the CIR(A) annulled the order-in-original and directed the DCIR to re-examine the submissions after affording the appellant a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

This decision represents a significant milestone, and we are pleased with the outcome. Should you require further clarification or assistance regarding this matter, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Thank you for your trust and cooperation throughout this process. We look forward to continuing to serve your needs effectively.

Warm regards,

Federation of Pakistan, the LHC has held that the objection of charging of further tax is to incentivize a person to register and implies that the person in under a lawful obligation to obtain registration number and has for some reason failed to do so. For your reference, the operating paragraph is reproduced below.

“The purpose of section 3(1A) imposing further tax on a person who fails to obtain registration number is to incentivize such a person to register and implies that the person in under a lawful obligation to obtain registration number and has for some reason failed to do so. This carrot and stick policy is to induce a person to register and also to enforce the legislative intent of registering person making taxable supplies. On a policy level, the wisdom behind this is to move towards a more documentary economy and help expand the tax base. Petitioners, who do not make taxable supplies under the law are under no legal obligation to register and, therefore, section 3(1A) does not relate to them. The petitioner cannot be burdened with the charge be burdened with the charge of further tax for not doing an act they are, under the law, not supposed to do. Unless, of course, the law undergoes an amendment of this effect.


5.	In another case of a taxpayer reported as 2021 PTD 1608 in case of Muhammad Arif Ice Factory v. Federation of Pakistan, the LHC has held further tax is applicable to a case a person is engaged in making taxable supplies and is no liable to be registered under the Act. While giving the decision, the LHC has held that:

“7.	In support of his contention for an answer in affirmative to the above question, learned counsel for respondents Nos. 2 and 3 has relied upon the provisions of sections 2(25) and 14(2) of the Act, which are reproduced herein below:

S.2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context,

(25) “registered person” means who is registered or is liable to be registered under this Act:

Provided that a person who is liable to be registered but not registered under this Act shall not be entitled to any benefit available to a registered person under any of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder.

The word “liable” used in the above provision has not been defined by the legistature in the Act. The word “liable” has been interpreted by the august Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Noon Sugar Mills Limited v. Commissioner of Income Tax (PLD 1990 SC 1156) to mean “subject to an obligation”. Applying the above interpretation to the expression “liable to be registered” as used in Section 2(25) of the Act would mean the person who has an obligation to be registered under the law.

………………………………………………………….

Person who are not registered under the Act fall in two distinct classes: firstly, those who are not required by law to be registered under the Act; secondly, those who are liable to be registered under the Act but have failed to register. For the purposes of “further tax” or “extra tax” under the Act, any interpretation that refuses to take into account the above classification and purports to imposes these taxes on both classes of persons renders the same taxes ex-facie discrimination in such a case would ensue from the lack of classification and similar treatment extended to dissimilarly or differently placed persons. Reliance is placed on Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala (AIR 1961 SC 552); State of Andhra Pradesh v. Nalla Raja Reddy (AIR 1967 SC 1458) and State of Kerala v. Haji K. Kutty Naha and others (AIR 1969 SC 378).

	Likewise, burdening those with imposition of “further tax” and “extra tax” who are not liable to be registered under the Act result in violation of the fundamental rights to property, as guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution. Reliance is placed on Federation of Pakistan v. Shaukat Ali Mian (PLD 1999 SC 1026).

18.	Theory of reading down is a rule of interpretation resorted to whenever a statutory provision, when read literally, leads to any violation of a fundamental right, or renders it without legislative competence, and courts read such a provision narrowly to save it from invalidity. Reading down is squarely applicable in this case to prevent violation of Articles 23, 24 and 25 of the Constitution. Resultantly, a restrictive meaning is to the application of section 3(1A) and section 3(5) of the Act read with Notification SRO 509(I)/2013 dated 12.06.2013 to those cases where the person was liable to be registered but has failed to register. Reliance is placed on Indus Jute Mills Ltd. through Chief Executive v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Finance, Islamabad and 3 others (2009 PTD 1473), Al-Karam CNF and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2011 PTD 1) and Syed Mushahid Shah v. F.I.A. (2017 SCMR 121*)

### Master File Requirements

The Master File provides an overview of the multinational enterprise (MNE) group's global operations and transfer pricing policies. Key requirements include:

1. **Organizational Structure**:
   - Chart of the MNE's legal and ownership structure.
   - List of constituent entities, their tax residences, and main business activities.

2. **Business Description**:
   - Description of the MNE's primary profit drivers.
   - Supply chain details for the group’s top five products/services.
   - Main geographic markets.
   - Functional analysis of value contributions by individual entities.

3. **Intangible Assets**:
   - Strategy for development, ownership, and exploitation of intangibles.
   - List of key intangibles and their legal owners.
   - Transfer pricing policies for R&D and intangibles.

4. **Intercompany Financial Activities**:
   - Description of the MNE's financing arrangements.
   - Identification of entities providing central financing functions.

5. **Financial and Tax Positions**:
   - Annual consolidated financial statements.
   - List and description of existing unilateral advance pricing agreements (APAs) and tax rulings.

### Local File Requirements

The Local File focuses on specific intercompany transactions and financial activities of the local entity. Key requirements include:

1. **Local Entity Information**:
   - Description of the local entity’s management structure and business strategy.
   - Information on key competitors.

2. **Material Intercompany Transactions**:
   - Description of material intercompany transactions.
   - Amount of intra-group payments and receipts for each transaction category.

3. **Comparability and Functional Analysis**:
   - Detailed functional analysis of the local entity's contributions.
   - Transfer pricing methods applied for each transaction category.
   - Comparable data and analysis.

4. **Financial Information**:
   - Financial statements for the fiscal year.
   - Link between financial data used in transfer pricing and annual financial statements.
   - Summary of financial data for comparables used in the analysis.

These requirements ensure that tax authorities have a comprehensive understanding of an MNE's transfer pricing practices, promoting compliance with the arm's length principle and reducing tax base erosion and profit shifting risks.

### Detailed Justification for KE's Services Being Covered Under "Commission Agent" as per Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011

#### Understanding of the Agreement Between KMC and KE:

The Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) has appointed K-Electric Limited (KE) as its collecting agent for Municipal Utility Charges and Tax (MUCT) in Karachi. Under the terms of this agreement:

- **Collection of MUCT**: KE is responsible for collecting MUCT from electricity consumers through their monthly electricity bills.
- **Service Fee**: KE charges a 7.5% service fee for the collection of MUCT.
- **Deduction of Dues**: KE deducts KMC's electricity dues from the total MUCT collected.
- **Transfer of Funds**: The remaining funds are transferred to KMC's designated account on a monthly basis.
- **Provision of Rates**: KMC provides the rates for MUCT and notifies KE of any changes.
- **Billing Corrections and Reports**: KE handles billing corrections and provides monthly collection reports to KMC.

#### Definition of "Commission Agent" under the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011:

According to the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011, a "commission agent" is defined as:

“Commission agent” means a person who acts on behalf of another person for causing sale or purchase of goods or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration, and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person,--
(i) deals with goods or services or documents of title to such goods or services; or
(ii) collects payment of sale price of such goods or services; or
(iii) guarantees for collection or payment for such goods or services; or
(iv) undertakes any activity relating to such sale or purchase of such goods or provision or receipt of such services.

#### Analysis and Justification:

**1. Acting on Behalf of Another Person:**

KE acts on behalf of KMC in collecting MUCT charges from electricity consumers. This is a central element of the definition of a commission agent. KE is providing this service to KMC for a consideration, which is the 7.5% service fee. This fee represents the compensation KE receives for performing the service of collecting MUCT charges.

**2. Collects Payment of Sale Price of Services:**

Clause (ii) of the definition explicitly includes any person who "collects payment of sale price of such goods or services." In this case, KE collects MUCT charges, which are payments for municipal utility services, on behalf of KMC. This aligns directly with the role of a commission agent as per the definition.

**3. Guarantees for Collection or Payment for Such Goods or Services:**

While KE does not directly guarantee the payment itself, it ensures the collection process is managed efficiently. KE deducts KMC's electricity dues from the total amount collected, which can be seen as an indirect guarantee of the collection of those dues. This responsibility ensures that KMC receives its due funds after the deduction of KE’s service fee and the electricity dues.

**4. Undertakes Any Activity Relating to Such Provision or Receipt of Services:**

Clause (iv) includes any activity related to the provision or receipt of services. KE’s role involves several such activities:
- **Billing Corrections**: KE handles any necessary corrections to the billing, ensuring accurate collection and reporting of MUCT charges.
- **Monthly Collection Reports**: KE provides monthly reports detailing the collections, deductions, and transfers, ensuring transparency and accountability in the process.

**Further Detailed Justifications:**

**Legal and Contractual Obligations:**
The agreement between KMC and KE is a formal arrangement where KE is contractually obliged to act on behalf of KMC. This legal relationship further solidifies KE’s position as a commission agent under the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011.

**Consideration for Services:**
The 7.5% service fee charged by KE is a direct consideration for the service of collecting MUCT charges. This fee is a classic example of a commission that a commission agent would earn for services rendered.

**Indirect Benefits and Compliance:**
KE’s role ensures compliance with municipal regulations and provides a streamlined process for KMC to collect its dues without directly engaging with each consumer. This benefits KMC by reducing administrative overhead and ensuring timely collection and transfer of funds.

**Alignment with Commission Agent Definition:**
- **Dealing with Services (Clause i)**: KE deals with the provision of billing and collection services.
- **Collects Payment (Clause ii)**: KE collects payments (MUCT charges) on behalf of KMC.
- **Guarantees for Collection (Clause iii)**: KE ensures the collection process is managed efficiently, indirectly guaranteeing the collection of dues.
- **Related Activities (Clause iv)**: KE undertakes various activities related to the collection and reporting of MUCT charges.

#### Conclusion:

Based on the understanding of the agreement and the detailed analysis of the definition of a "commission agent" as per the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011, it is evident that KE’s services for the collection of MUCT charges on behalf of KMC fall under the category of a commission agent. KE acts on behalf of KMC, collects payments for services, and performs related activities, all of which justify the classification of these services as those of a commission agent. Consequently, the 7.5% service fee charged by KE for these activities would be subject to Sindh Sales Tax.

### Master File Requirements

The Master File provides an overview of the multinational enterprise (MNE) group's global business operations, transfer pricing policies, and the overall compliance framework. The primary requirements typically include:

1. **Organizational Structure**:
   - A chart illustrating the MNE's legal and ownership structure.
   - A list of all the constituent entities, their country of tax residence, and the nature of their main business activities.

2. **Business Description**:
   - A description of the MNE's principal drivers of business profit.
   - A description of the supply chain for the group’s five largest products and/or service offerings.
   - A description of the main geographic markets for the group’s products and services.
   - A detailed functional analysis describing the principal contributions to value creation by individual entities within the group.

3. **Intangible Assets**:
   - A description of the MNE's overall strategy for the development, ownership, and exploitation of intangibles.
   - A list of intangibles or groups of intangibles important for transfer pricing purposes, and which entities legally own them.
   - A description of the MNE's transfer pricing policies for R&D and intangibles.

4. **Intercompany Financial Activities**:
   - A description of how the MNE is financed, including significant financing arrangements with unrelated lenders.
   - Identification of any members of the MNE group that provide a central financing function.

5. **Financial and Tax Positions**:
   - The MNE's annual consolidated financial statements.
   - A list and description of the MNE's existing unilateral advance pricing agreements (APAs) and other tax rulings relating to the allocation of income among countries.

### Local File Requirements

The Local File provides detailed information on specific intercompany transactions and financial activities of the local entity, ensuring that these transactions comply with the arm's length principle. The primary requirements typically include:

1. **Local Entity Information**:
   - A detailed description of the local entity’s management structure.
   - A detailed description of the business and business strategy.
   - Information on key competitors.

2. **Material Intercompany Transactions**:
   - A description of material intercompany transactions (both domestic and international) involving the local entity.
   - The amount of intra-group payments and receipts for each category of transactions involving the local entity (e.g., products, services, royalties, interest, etc.).

3. **Comparability and Functional Analysis**:
   - A detailed functional analysis outlining the contributions of the local entity to the value creation of the MNE group.
   - Information on the transfer pricing method applied for each category of intercompany transactions.
   - Comparable data and analysis used to justify the transfer pricing.

4. **Financial Information**:
   - Financial information on the local entity, including financial statements for the fiscal year concerned.
   - Information on how the financial data used in applying the transfer pricing method can be tied to the annual financial statements.
   - Summary schedules of relevant financial data for comparables used in the analysis.

These requirements are designed to provide tax authorities with a comprehensive view of an MNE's transfer pricing policies and practices, ensuring compliance with the arm's length principle and minimizing the risk of tax base erosion and profit shifting.

Subject: Clarification on Applicability and Exceptions of Section 4AB

Dear [Client's Name],

I hope this email finds you well.

Following our recent discussion regarding the applicability and exceptions under Section 4AB, please find below our detailed responses and clarifications:

1. **Deductible Expenses (Zakat/Donations to Accredited Institutions)**:
   - Deductible expenses such as Zakat or donations to accredited institutions will reduce the annual taxable amount of the employee. Accordingly, Section 4AB will be adjusted to reflect the reduced taxable income.

2. **Surcharge Adjustments and Taxable Income Below Rs. 10M**:
   - It is an accepted fact that any surcharge already deducted is non-refundable. However, if deductible expenses reduce the taxable income below Rs. 10 million, Section 4AB will no longer be applicable for the remaining period’s salary of the employee.

3. **Tax Credit for Investment in Approved Pension Funds**:
   - Tax credits against investments in approved pension funds will affect the calculation of Section 4AB. The surcharge will be computed on the revised tax assessed, considering the tax credit as per the mechanism provided under Section 63 of the Ordinance.

4. **Advance Tax Adjustments**:
   - Advance tax adjustments arising from the purchase of vehicles, immovable property, etc., do not affect the calculation of Section 4AB. The surcharge is calculated on the gross tax value, excluding such advance payments.

5. **Impact of Tax Adjustments on Section 4AB**:
   - Any adjustments in the normal tax liability of the employee will account for the subsequent decrease in the liability calculation under Section 4AB. The surcharge will be recalculated based on the updated taxable salary.

6. **Understanding and Feedback on Section 4AB**:
   - Section 4AB is introduced as a surcharge with no adjustment other than deductible expenses allowed. The calculation of Section 4AB will be based on the annual gross salary. We seek your feedback on this understanding and the calculations shared above.

Our Responses:

- Your understanding is correct. The surcharge is levied on tax computed under Division I, Part I of the First Schedule to the Ordinance. Therefore, Zakat paid is deductible in terms of Section 60 of the Ordinance for computing the taxable salary.
- The taxes of employees are assessed on an annual basis, and the employer must account for the annual salary for withholding purposes under Section 149 of the Ordinance. The Finance Act, 2024 has amended Section 149 to include the effect of the surcharge under Section 4AB. Thus, the employer must account for the surcharge (if applicable) while withholding income tax. If the taxable salary is estimated to remain below the Rs. 10 million threshold, no surcharge will be computed. However, any changes in salary scales or admissible credits during the year will lead to a recalculation, and the revised surcharge (if applicable) will be withheld over the remaining months of the financial year.
- Section 63 provides the mechanism to compute tax credit on contributions to an approved Pension Fund. According to Section 2(63) of the Ordinance, 'tax' includes any tax imposed under Chapter II, penalties, fees, or other charges. Hence, the surcharge falls within this definition, and tax credits under Section 63 should consider the surcharge.
- Advance tax paid on vehicles/immovable property is not considered when levying the surcharge under Section 4AB. These are not credits/admissible expenses against salary tax but rather a mechanism for advance payment.
- The annual taxable salary can change during the year, affecting the tax liability (including surcharge). If the taxable salary falls below Rs. 10 million due to deductible allowances, the revised tax liability (excluding surcharge) will be computed and spread over the remaining months of the financial year.
- The surcharge is levied on tax computed under Division I, Part I of the First Schedule. No specific deductions are allowable except those already provided under the Ordinance.

### Justification for KE's Services Being Covered Under "Commission Agent" as per Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011

**Understanding of the Agreement Between KMC and KE:**

The Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) has appointed K-Electric Limited (KE) as the collecting agent for Municipal Utility Charges and Tax (MUCT) in Karachi. Under this agreement, KE is responsible for collecting MUCT from electricity consumers through their monthly bills. KE charges a 7.5% service fee for this collection service and deducts KMC's electricity dues from the total collected amount. The remaining funds are transferred to KMC's designated account on a monthly basis. KMC provides the rates and notifies KE of any changes, while KE handles billing corrections and provides monthly collection reports to KMC.

**Definition of "Commission Agent" under the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011:**

According to the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011, a "commission agent" is defined as follows:

“Commission agent” means a person who acts on behalf of another person for causing sale or purchase of goods or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration, and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person,--
(i) deals with goods or services or documents of title to such goods or services; or
(ii) collects payment of sale price of such goods or services; or
(iii) guarantees for collection or payment for such goods or services; or
(iv) undertakes any activity relating to such sale or purchase of such goods or provision or receipt of such services.

**Analysis and Justification:**

KE's role in collecting MUCT charges on behalf of KMC aligns with several elements of the "commission agent" definition under the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011:

1. **Acting on Behalf of Another Person:**
   KE acts on behalf of KMC by collecting MUCT charges from electricity consumers. This is a key aspect of the commission agent definition, as KE is providing a service to KMC for a consideration (7.5% service fee).

2. **Collecting Payment of Sale Price of Services:**
   Clause (ii) of the commission agent definition explicitly includes any person who "collects payment of sale price of such goods or services." In this context, KE collects MUCT charges, which are payments for municipal utility services, on behalf of KMC.

3. **Guarantees for Collection or Payment for Such Goods or Services:**
   While KE does not guarantee the payment itself, it ensures the collection process is handled efficiently and deducts KMC's electricity dues from the total collected amount, thus partially guaranteeing the effective collection and transfer of funds to KMC.

4. **Undertakes Any Activity Relating to Such Provision or Receipt of Services:**
   KE's responsibilities include billing corrections and providing monthly collection reports. These activities are directly related to the provision and receipt of the MUCT collection service, fitting within the scope of clause (iv) of the commission agent definition.

**Conclusion:**

Based on the understanding of the agreement between KMC and KE, and the definition of a "commission agent" as per the Sindh Sales Tax Act, 2011, KE's services for the collection of MUCT charges on behalf of KMC are covered under the commission agent category. KE acts on behalf of KMC, collects payments for services, and undertakes related activities, all of which justify the classification of these services as those of a commission agent. Consequently, the 7.5% service fee charged by KE for these activities would be subject to Sindh Sales Tax.

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 of Pakistan, a wholesaler is generally defined as a person who purchases goods in bulk from manufacturers or producers and sells them in large quantities to retailers, other wholesalers, or various businesses. Here is a more detailed explanation:

### Definition of Wholesaler:
- **Wholesaler**: A person or entity that purchases goods in large quantities from manufacturers or producers and sells them in smaller quantities to retailers, industrial, commercial, institutional, or other professional business users. The key characteristic of a wholesaler is that they do not sell directly to the end consumer but rather to other businesses that will either use or resell the goods.

### Characteristics of Wholesalers:
1. **Bulk Purchasing**: Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities, which allows them to get products at lower prices.
2. **Resale in Large Quantities**: They sell the goods in quantities that are smaller than what they purchase but still significant compared to retail sales.
3. **Business Customers**: Their primary customers are other businesses, such as retailers, other wholesalers, industrial users, and commercial institutions.

### Relevant Sections in the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001:
While the Ordinance does not always explicitly define every term, wholesalers are generally understood in the context of:
- **Section 153**: This section relates to payments for goods and services and the withholding tax regime. Wholesalers, like other businesses, may be subject to withholding tax obligations when making payments for goods and services.
- **Section 23**: This section pertains to deductions for certain expenses and may impact wholesalers in terms of allowable deductions and accounting for inventory.
- **Part II of the First Schedule**: This part outlines the rates of tax for different types of income, which would include business income derived by wholesalers.

### Practical Implications:
- **Withholding Tax**: Wholesalers are often required to withhold tax on payments for supplies and services, according to the rates specified under the Ordinance.
- **Filing Requirements**: They must file tax returns and maintain records of their transactions, including purchases and sales, to comply with the tax regulations.
- **Deductible Expenses**: Wholesalers can claim deductions for expenses incurred in the course of their business, subject to the provisions of the Ordinance.

In summary, under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, wholesalers are entities involved in the bulk purchase and sale of goods to other businesses rather than directly to end consumers. They play a crucial role in the supply chain and are subject to specific tax obligations and benefits under the Ordinance.

### Summary of Rule 108: Transactions Between Associates

Rule 108 empowers the Commissioner to adjust income, deductions, or tax credits between associated persons to reflect the income that would have been realized in an arm’s length transaction. The Commissioner can also determine the source and nature of any income, payment, or loss as revenue, capital, or otherwise when making these adjustments. Taxpayers engaged in transactions with associates are required to maintain a master file and a local file containing prescribed documents and information, keep and furnish a country-by-country report where applicable, and retain all necessary documents and information for a specified period. If requested by the Commissioner, taxpayers must provide these documents within thirty days. The Commissioner may grant an extension for submission, up to forty-five days, with longer extensions allowed only under exceptional circumstances.

It is pertinent to mention that as per section 108 of the Ordinance, taxpayers engaged in transactions with associates are required to maintain a master file and a local file containing prescribed documents and information, keep and furnish a country-by-country report where applicable, and retain all necessary documents and information for a specified period. Master File Requirements: The Master File provides an overview of the multinational enterprise (MNE) group's global operations and transfer pricing policies. Key requirements include:
Organizational Structure:
   - Chart of the MNE's legal and ownership structure.
   - List of constituent entities, their tax residences, and main business activities.
 
Business Description:
   - Description of the MNE's primary profit drivers.
   - Supply chain details for the group’s top five products/services.
   - Main geographic markets.
   - Functional analysis of value contributions by individual entities.
 
Intercompany Financial Activities:
   - Description of the MNE's financing arrangements.
   - Identification of entities providing central financing functions.
 
Financial and Tax Positions:
   - Annual consolidated financial statements.
   - List and description of existing unilateral advance pricing agreements (APAs) and tax rulings.
 
Local File Requirements: The Local File focuses on specific intercompany transactions and financial activities of the local entity. Key requirements include:
Local Entity Information:
   - Description of the local entity’s management structure and business strategy.
   - Information on key competitors.
 
Material Intercompany Transactions:
   - Description of material intercompany transactions.
   - Amount of intra-group payments and receipts for each transaction category.
 
Comparability and Functional Analysis:
   - Detailed functional analysis of the local entity's contributions.
   - Transfer pricing methods applied for each transaction category.
   - Comparable data and analysis.
 
Financial Information:
   - Financial statements for the fiscal year.
   - Link between financial data used in transfer pricing and annual financial statements.
   - Summary of financial data for comparables used in the analysis.
 
These requirements ensure that tax authorities have a comprehensive understanding of an MNE's transfer pricing practices, promoting compliance with the arm's length principle and reducing tax base erosion and profit shifting risks.

Please prepare email to client on the following discussion with respect to applicability/exceptions in case of Section 4AB:

•	Deductible expenses (Zakat/Donation to Accredited Institutions) will reduce the annual taxable amount of employee and section 4AB will be adjusted accordingly.

•	It is accepted fact that whatever surcharge already deducted is non-refundable but what If deductible expenses in some cases decreases taxable income below 10M mark, will the section 4AB still be applicable on the remaining period salary of the employee? 


•	In case of Tax Credit against investment in approve pension fund. Will the amount of tax adjusted also affects Section 4AB or it will remain calculated on the gross value of tax?

•	In case of Advance Tax adjustment arises from purchase of Vehicle or Immovable Property etc. Will the amount of tax adjusted also affects Section 4AB or it will remain calculated on the gross value of tax?

•	Any tax adjustment in the normal tax liability of employee will or will not account for subsequent decrease in liability calculation under section 4AB?

•	As per our understanding, section 4AB is introduced as surcharge, and no adjustment other than deductible expenses is allowable, calculation of section 4AB will be done on Annual gross salary. We require your feedback on the points and calculation being shared above.


Our Responses: 

Yes - Your understanding is correct. The surcharge has been levied on tax computed under Division-I, Part-I of First Schedule to the Ordinance. Therefore, Zakat paid is deductible in terms of section 60 of the Ordinance for the purpose of computing the taxable salary. 

The taxes of employees are required to be assessed on annual basis and employer is required to account for the annual salary of employees for the purpose of withholding under section 149 of the Ordinance. Though Finance Act, 2024, section 149 has also been amended to give the effect of surcharge levied under section (4AB). Therefore, employer is required to account for surcharge (if applicable) while making the income tax withholding. In case, where taxable salary is estimated not to cross the annual threshold of Rs. 10 million, no surcharge would be computed. However, owing to changes / revision in salary scales or admissible credits during the year, the taxable salary would be recomputed actualizing the updated amounts. Accordingly, the revised slab and surcharge (if applicable) would be levied, and tax would be withheld during the remaining months of financial year. 

Section 63 provides the mechanism to compute the tax credit on contribution to an approved Pension Fund. The relevant extract of section 63(2) of the Ordinance are reproduced as under:

	“(A/B) * C
	Where--

A	is the amount of tax assessed to the person for the tax year before allowance of any tax credit under this Part;
 	
	B	is the person’s taxable income of the tax year; and

	C	is the lesser of –

(i)	the total contribution or premium referred to in sub-section (1) paid by the person in the year; or

(ii)	………….” 
        (underlining is ours)
			
In terms of section 2(63) of the Ordinance the expression ‘tax’ has very widely been defined to mean “any tax imposed under Chapter II and includes any penalty, fee or other charge or any sum or amount leviable or payable under this Ordinance’. Thus, surcharge clearly falls within the ambit of expression ‘tax’ as defined therein. Therefore, in terms of section 63, tax credit is to be computed on the basis of ‘tax assessed’ in the manner above. Thus, in our view, surcharge is to be considered for computing tax credit under section 63 of the Ordinance.  

The advance tax paid on vehicle / immovable property would not be considered while levying the surcharge under section 4AB of the Ordinance. These advance taxes are not credits / admissible expenses against the tax on salary but discharge of liability through mechanism of advance payment. 

As stated above, the annual taxable salary can change during the year and accordingly, the tax liability (including surcharge) can also vary. Therefore, in case of decrease in taxable salary below Rs. 10 million due to deductible allowances, the revised tax liability (excluding surcharge) would be computed and the net tax liability would be spread over the remaining months of the financial year.

The surcharge has been levied on tax computed under Division I, Part I of First Schedule. No specific deduction is allowable except for those which are already available under the Ordinance.

### Summary of Income Tax Updates

**Surcharge:**
For individuals and AOPs with taxable income over Rs 10 million, a surcharge of 10% on income tax is applicable. For instance, with a taxable income of Rs 12 million, the surcharge would be Rs 346,500. Employers must withhold this surcharge from salaries. This surcharge does not apply to incomes under the final tax regime or those with special tax rates, such as capital gains on listed securities and immovable properties. For taxpayers liable to pay super tax, the surcharge applies only to their normal income tax liability.

**Restriction on Foreign Travels for Non-Filers:**
Section 114B empowers the FBR to restrict foreign travel for Pakistani citizens not on the Active Taxpayers’ List (ATL), except for those holding NICOPs, minors, students, and persons traveling for Hajj or Umrah.

**Assets of Spouse in Wealth Statement:**
Assets of a spouse will be included in a person's wealth statement only if the spouse is dependent.

**Increase in Tax/Withholding on Dividend:**
Tax and withholding rates on dividends from mutual funds with 50% or more income from profit on debt have increased from 15% to 25%.

**Tax Rates on Disposal of Listed Securities:**
Capital gains tax on listed securities acquired after July 1, 2024, is set at a flat rate of 15% for ATL filers. Non-ATL filers face a higher rate or slab rates specified in Division I of Part I of the First Schedule.

**Capital Gains Tax on Immovable Property:**
For properties acquired after July 1, 2024, a flat rate of 15% capital gains tax applies to ATL filers. Non-ATL filers face progressive tax rates with a minimum of 15%. For properties acquired before July 1, 2024, the previous tax rates based on holding periods remain in effect.

**Withholding Tax Rates for Telephone and Internet Users:**
The withholding tax rate for non-ATL individuals on telephone and internet bills has increased from 15% to 75%.

**Advance Tax on Property Transactions:**
Progressive advance tax rates on the purchase/sale of properties are introduced based on ATL status and filing history. Late filers face higher rates than ATL filers but lower than non-ATL filers.

**Tenth Schedule (Rates of Tax for Non-Filers):**
For non-ATL individuals, advance tax rates on motor vehicles and property purchases have increased by 200% and 250%, respectively. For other taxes, the rate is increased by 100%. This also applies to withholding taxes not prescribed in the First Schedule, such as capital gains on shares.

**Enhanced Withholding Taxes from Non-Filers:**
The withholding tax rates for non-ATL individuals have increased as follows:
- Section 151: From 30% to 35% on profit on debt.
- Section 236G: From 0.2% to 2% on sales to distributors, dealers, or wholesalers (except fertilizers).
- Section 236H: From 1% to 2.5% on sales to retailers.

Capital gains on listed shares and other securities are excluded from general enhanced withholding tax provisions.

In accordance with section 12 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance], coupled with section 101 of the Ordinance, salary constitutes Pakistan-source income to the extent that it is received from any employment "exercised" within Pakistan, irrespective of where it is paid.

Additionally, as outlined in section 12(2)(e)((iii) of the Ordinance, any profits received in lieu of, or in addition to, salary or wages—including amounts received upon termination of employment, whether voluntarily or under agreement, encompassing compensation for redundancy or loss of employment and golden handshake payments—are considered part of the salary.

Considering the above, it is imperative to note that in your case, the severance package will be regarded as part of the salary as defined in section 12(2)(e)((iii) of the Ordinance. Consequently, this salary income should be apportioned between employment exercised within and outside Pakistan, with only the portion related to employment in Pakistan being taxable.

Furthermore, we strongly recommend obtaining a letter from the HR Department clarifying the nature of the severance package. This letter should explicitly state that the specified amount pertains to both employment within and outside Pakistan, thereby providing a clear delineation of the amount attributed to each. This precautionary measure will help prevent any potential confusion or discrepancies in the future.

The provisions of Section 65B, specifically relating to the tax credit under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, can be interpreted with reference to its applicability and implications for business investments in modernization, expansion, and balancing.

### Eligibility for Tax Credit under Section 65B
Section 65B provides a tax credit to companies for investments in industrial undertakings that are engaged in the setting up of new manufacturing facilities or the expansion of existing ones. This credit is allowed against the tax payable and is calculated as a percentage of the amount invested.

### Key Provisions:
1. **Eligible Investments**: The tax credit under Section 65B applies to investments made for the purchase of plant and machinery used in Pakistan. The purpose of the investment must be for the balancing, modernization, or expansion of the industrial undertaking.

2. **Period of Investment**: The credit is allowed for investments made between July 1, 2010, and June 30, 2021, according to the amendments and extensions in the law.

3. **Credit Rate**: The rate of the tax credit varies depending on the year of the investment. For example, the rate was initially set at 10% and may have been adjusted through subsequent amendments.

4. **Set-off Mechanism**: The credit is allowed to be set off against the tax payable for the tax year in which the investment was made and may be carried forward to the subsequent tax years if the full amount of the credit is not utilized in the year of investment.

### Implications for Companies:
- **Reduction in Tax Liability**: By claiming this credit, companies can significantly reduce their tax liability for the year in which the qualifying investment is made.
  
- **Encouragement for Investment**: This section is designed to encourage companies to invest in their infrastructure by offering a tax incentive, thereby contributing to industrial growth.

- **Documentation and Compliance**: Companies must maintain detailed records of the investments made, including the nature of the assets purchased and their usage, to substantiate the claim for this tax credit. Additionally, adherence to the conditions set forth in the Ordinance is crucial to avoid disallowance.

The apportionment of input tax is a crucial aspect of the Sales Tax Rules, specifically targeting registered persons who engage in both taxable and exempt supplies. These provisions are designed to ensure that the input tax credit is correctly allocated, thereby preventing any undue claims and promoting compliance with tax laws.

Under the apportionment rules, input tax paid on raw materials that are exclusively used for taxable supplies is fully admissible. This means that when raw materials are dedicated solely to the production of taxable goods or services, the entire input tax can be claimed as a credit. Conversely, input tax paid on raw materials used exclusively for exempt supplies is not admissible. If the raw materials contribute solely to exempt goods or services, no input tax credit can be claimed. 

When raw materials are used for both taxable and exempt supplies, the input tax must be apportioned between the two. This is done using a specific formula that calculates the portion of input tax attributable to taxable supplies. The formula ensures that only the appropriate amount of input tax is claimed, reflecting the actual use of the materials.

Adjustments to input tax are made on a monthly basis, but these adjustments are provisional. At the end of each financial year, a final adjustment is required based on the actual taxable and exempt supplies made during the year. This process ensures that the input tax credit claimed accurately reflects the business's activities over the year.

It is important to note that any incorrect application of the apportionment formula or wrongful claims of input tax, even if initially treated as provisional, can result in penalties under the law. Therefore, it is essential to apply the formula accurately and make the necessary adjustments to avoid any legal repercussions. By following these rules, businesses can manage their input tax credits effectively while ensuring full compliance with tax regulations.

**General Write-Up on Apportionment of Input Tax**

The apportionment of input tax is a key provision in the Sales Tax Rules, specifically designed for registered persons who simultaneously make both taxable and exempt supplies. Understanding and applying these rules correctly is essential for ensuring compliance with tax laws and optimizing input tax credit.

### 1. **Application of Apportionment Rules**
The rules outlined in this chapter apply to registered taxpayers engaged in making both taxable and exempt supplies. These provisions ensure that the input tax credit is correctly apportioned between taxable and exempt supplies, preventing any undue claims of input tax.

### 2. **Determination of Input Tax**
   - **Input Tax on Taxable Supplies:** Input tax paid on raw materials exclusively related to taxable supplies is fully admissible under the law. This means that if the raw materials are solely used for producing taxable goods or services, the entire input tax can be claimed.
   - **Input Tax on Exempt Supplies:** Conversely, input tax paid on raw materials solely related to exempt supplies is not admissible. If the raw materials are used exclusively for producing exempt goods or services, no input tax credit can be claimed.
   - **Input Tax for Both Exempt and Taxable Supplies:** When raw materials are used for producing both taxable and exempt supplies, the input tax must be apportioned. The formula provided under the rules ensures that only the appropriate portion of the input tax is claimed against the taxable supplies.

### 3. **Apportionment Formula**
The apportionment of input tax for supplies that are both exempt and taxable is calculated using the following formula:

\[
\text{Input Tax on Taxable Supplies} = \frac{\text{Value of Taxable Supplies}}{\text{Value of Taxable + Exempt Supplies}} \times \text{Residual Input Tax}
\]

This formula helps determine the input tax credit that can be claimed in relation to taxable supplies, ensuring compliance and accuracy in tax reporting.

### 4. **Monthly and Final Adjustments**
The adjustment of input tax is done on a monthly basis, and it is treated as provisional throughout the financial year. At the end of each financial year, a final adjustment must be made based on the actual taxable and exempt supplies made during that period. This ensures that the input tax credit claimed aligns with the actual business activities of the taxpayer.

### 5. **Penalties for Incorrect Adjustment**
Incorrect application of the apportionment formula or wrongful claims of input tax credit, even if initially provisional, can lead to penalties under the relevant provisions of the law. Therefore, it is crucial to apply the formula correctly and make accurate adjustments to avoid any legal consequences.

By adhering to these rules, businesses can effectively manage their input tax credits while ensuring compliance with the applicable tax laws.

We refer to the email of your Mr. Muhammad Arsalan Shaukat dated July 15, 2024 whereby we have been required to comment whether the Company falls under the definition of manufacturer prescribed under the provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Ordinance) and whether the following customers of the Company be considered as Company's dealers/ distributors in terms of the provisions of section 236G of the Ordinance as amended vide Finance Act, 2024.

•	Attock Refinery Limited (ARL), Parco Refinery, National Refinery Limited (NRL), Pakistan Refinery Limited (PRL) & EPRF Refinery [Refineries] for supply of Crude Oil.

•	Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) and Sui Northern Gas Pipeline Limited (SNGPL) for purchase of Gas produced and manufactured by the Company.

•	LPG marketing companies licensed by Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) for sale of Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG). 

•	Sale Sulphur from Dakhni condensate after processing to various companies through bidding which is used by these companies in their industrial process.

3.	We give below our comments which are from the Income Tax point of view based on existing provisions of the Ordinance and are based on the understanding given to us that the Company supply crude oil without any processing.

4.1	In this respect, we wish to inform you that under the provisions of Section 153(7)(iv) of the Ordinance a manufacturer has been defined to mean a person who is engaged in the production or manufacturing of goods, which includes any process in which an article singly or in combination with material, components is either converted into another distinct article or product is so changed, transferred or reshaped that it becomes capable of being put to use differently or distinctly or  process of assembling, mixing, cutting or preparation of goods in any other manner. Section 153(7)(iv) of the Ordinance is reproduced below:

(iv) “manufacturer” means a person who is engaged in production or manufacturing of goods, which includes—

a)	any process in which an article singly or in combination with other articles, material, components, is either converted into another distinct article or product is so changed, transferred, or reshaped that it becomes capable of being put to use differently or distinctly; or 
b)	a process of assembling, mixing, cutting or preparation of goods in any other manner.

4.2	In view of the above and the understanding given to us, the Company would fall under the definition of manufacturer: 

•	in case of extraction and supply of crude oil by the Company to oil Refineries, since, the Company is not processing the said crude oil, it shall not fall in the definition of manufacturer.

•	In case of extraction, processing and supply of gas, since, the Company is changing the specifications of gas and then supplies it to its customers, it shall fall under the definition of manufacturer.

•	 In case of production of LPG, since the Company is producing the LPG during the processing of natural gas and condensate, it shall fall under the definition of manufacturer.

•	In case of production of Sulphur, since, the Company is producing it as a bi product during the processing of Dakhni condensate, it shall fall under the definition of manufacturer.

5.1	The term “distributor” has been defined to means a person who is appointed by the manufacturer or any other person for a specified area to purchase goods from the manufacturer for further supply. The term “distributor” is defined under section 2(18A) of the Ordinance, the relevant provisions of the section are reproduced below for ease of reference:

“(18A) “distributor” means a person appointed by a manufacturer, importer or any other person for a specified area to purchase goods from him for further supply.”

5.2	Further, the term “dealer” is not defined in the Income tax Ordinance. However, as per the general definition of the term dealer as defined in the Black Law Dictionary, it means the person who buys goods to sell again. The relevant definition is reproduced below for your ease of reference:

“dealer” A dealer, in the popular, and therefore in the statutory, sense of the word, is not one who buys to keep, or makes to sell, but one who buys to sell again.

5.3	Furthermore, we wish to inform you that the term “wholesaler” is not defined in the Ordinance, however, the term is defined in the subsection 47 of the Section 2 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (ST Act) and includes dealer and means any person who is engaged in the business of buying and selling goods by wholesale i.e., to sell by large parcels, generally in original packages and not by retail. The relevant provisions of Section 2(47) of the ST Act are reproduced below for you ease of reference:

(47) “wholesaler” includes a dealer and means any person who carries on, whether regularly or otherwise, the business of buying and selling goods by wholesale or of supplying or distributing goods, directly or indirectly, by wholesale for cash or deferred payment or for commission or other valuable consideration or stores such goods belonging to others as an agent for the purpose of sale; and includes a person supplying taxable goods to a person who deducts income tax at source under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

5.4	In respect of supply of crude oil by the Company to the oil Refineries, since as per our understanding above, the refineries are buying crude oil for refining. Accordingly, they will not fall under the definition of dealer/ distributor of the Company in terms of section 2(18A) read with section 236G of the Ordinance.

5.5.1	In respect of supply of Gas by the Company to SSGC and SNGPL, we understand that SSGC and SNGPL are engaged in the transmission, distribution, and sale of gas in the franchise areas of Sindh and Baluchistan and as per the gas sale purchase agreement read with the relevant Petroleum Concession Agreement, the gas is offered to the President of Pakistan (the President) and it is only the President who can purchase gas from the oil and gas exploration and production companies and for that purpose the President has specifically appointed/ nominated SSGC and SNGPL to act on its behalf for the purchase of gas. 

5.5.2	Further in this respect we refer to the Judgement issued by the Honorable Islamabad High Court vide order sheet dated October 5, 2023, whereby it has been held that the dealership relation/ agreement involves the payment of commission and where the revenue is recorded by the seller at the time of sale the relevant transaction is not a dealership transaction rather a sale purchase transaction. The relevant portion of the aforementioned order is reproduced below for your ease of reference:

“4. We have perused the decisions rendered by the Commissioner Appeals as well as the Tribunal. In relation to question No.1 the Commissioner Appeals analyzed the dealership agreement between the Taxpayer and the dealer and found that the relationship between the Taxpayer and the dealer had clearly been defined in Clause-19 of such agreement as that of buyer and seller. Further, such relationship was borne out by the fact that at the time of delivery of goods by the Taxpayer to the dealer, the revenue in relation thereto was booked by the Taxpayer in its books of account. On such basis, the Commissioner Appeals concluded that the relationship between the Taxpayer and the dealer was that of buyer and seller and the transaction was in the nature of sale and did not involve payment of commission. The Tribunal upheld such finding and we agree with the learned counsel for the Taxpayer that this finding of fact cannot be re-opened or second-guessed by this Court in its reference jurisdiction.” 

5.5.3	In view of the above we understand that, there is typically no “dealer-distributor” or “wholesaler” arrangement of SSGC and SNGPL with the Company and the common terms “wholesaler”/ “dealer”  and “ distributor” itself when considered in terms of the extent of operations of SSGC and SNGPL are distinguishable and a case is made out for non-application of advance tax collection as per section 236G of the Ordinance. Furthermore, the term “distributor” as stated in paragraph 5.1 above, further specifies that the distributor is a person who in engaged by the manufacturer, importer or any other person for selling the goods purchased from him in a specified area. As per our understanding, SSGC and SNGPL are buying the Gas from the Company for further supply, however, they are not appointed by the Company or any other supplier for a specified area for further supply of the goods.

5.5.4	It is, nevertheless, important to understand the legislative intent and purpose behind the introduction of the above-mentioned Section i.e., 236G in the Ordinance through Finance Bill 2013. To establish the same, we refer to the Salient features of the Finance Bill, 2013 wherein it was mentioned that contribution of the wholesale and retail sector towards the tax revenue does not commensurate with share of this sector in the GDP. To ensure documentation of the economy and to bring the traders into the tax net, all manufacturers were made liable to collect adjustable withholding tax from distributors, dealers, and wholesalers.

5.5.6	Considering the above, the legislative intent in the instant case appears to cover under its ambit the undocumented wholesale and retail sectors and not gas distribution companies like SSGC and SNGPL, being registered and documented sector. In case of SSGC and SNGPL, the sector is not only documented but regulated and there are licensing requirements as well. 

5.5.7	In view of the above, we understand that the SSGC and SNGPL are shall not be considered “distributor” to the Company and the provisions of Section 236G of the Ordinance shall not be applicable to SSGC and SNGPL as they are already registered for tax purposes and already paying the taxes due upon them. 

5.6	In respect of supply of LPG by the Company to LPG marketing companies, as per our understanding stated in paragraph 2 above, those LPG marketing companies are licensed by OGRA for purchase of LPG and sale of the same to their customers. Further, the terms of the agreements between the Company and those LPG marketing companies also reflect that the LPG marketing companies are not the Company’s distributors in terms of section 2(18A) read with section 236G of the Ordinance. 

5.7	In respect of supply of Sulphur by the Company to various companies/buyers, since as per our understanding stated in paragraph 2 above, these companies/buyers are buying the same for use in their industrial process and are not buying it for further supply, these companies/buyers shall not be treated as dealer/distributor of the Company in terms of section 2(18A) read with section 236G of the Ordinance. 

5.8	It is, however, cautioned that the tax department may not agree with the above interpretation and take a converse position. Owing to the said risk, we suggest that the Company should obtain commercial indemnity from above mentioned Companies subject to the condition that they will get their statuses verified from FBR within a specified timeframe in context of the section 236G, alternatively the Company may deduct tax under the aforementioned section 236G of the Ordinance.

Hi Walid, hope this email find you well.
We refer to earlier e-mails and subsequent discussion with you whereby you have requested our views on your specific queries as regards sections 236G and 236H of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [the Ordinance] in the light of the recent amendments proposed through the Finance Bill, 2024-2025 [FB 2024] announced on June 12, 2024.
The specific query for our consideration is whether advance tax under section 236G or 236H is required to be collected by UEPL from Sui Southern Gas Company Limited [SSGC], being the purchaser of Natural Gas.
SSGC is engaged in the transmission, distribution, and sale of gas in the franchise areas of Sindh and Baluchistan. As per the terms of the gas sale purchase agreement read with the relevant Petroleum Concession Agreements, the gas is offered to the President of Pakistan who has nominated SSGC to act on its behalf for the purchase of gas.
Section 236G mandates that "every manufacturer at the time of sale to distributors, dealers, and wholesalers shall collect advance tax." This is a requirement triggered only on sales made to these categories of persons and thus the relevant definitions need to be considered as to who qualifies as distributors, dealers, and wholesalers under the Ordinance.
Definition of “Distributor” under section 2(18A) of the Ordinance is: “Distributor means a person appointed by a manufacturer, importer or any other person for a specified area to purchase goods from him for further supply.”
There is requirement for a formal appointment by the manufacturer whereas between UEPL and SSGC there is no such arrangement. Sales terms are independent and non-obligatory and thus the UEPL’s sales case does not fall here.
Next, the terms ‘Dealers and Wholesalers’, which are not defined under the Ordinance.
Under legal terms: (source: Blacks’ law): “A dealer, in the popular, and therefore in the statutory, sense of the word, is not one who buys to keep, or makes to sell, but one who buys to sell again.”
(source: Merriams-Websters): “one that deals.”
Wholesale: To sell by wholesale, is to sell by large parcels, generally in original packages, and not by retail. 
Lastly, is the case of sale by SSGC to end consumers and any implication of Section 236H of the Ordinance. Section 236H mandates the collection of advance tax at the time of sale to retailers. This includes manufacturers, distributors, dealers, wholesalers, or commercial importers selling goods to entities classified as retailers. The section aims to ensure advance tax collection on sales made within the retail supply chain and retailers are specifically defined as entities engaged in selling goods to end consumers as part of their business operations.
A bare perusal of all the above definitions suggests that SSGC could come under the grab of both sections 236G and 236H. However, there are arguments to assert that neither section applies to SSGC:
SSGC is a licensed buyer of natural gas, specifically appointed/nominated by the President of Pakistan to purchase gas on its behalf. SSGC is a publicly listed company that operates under the administrative control of the Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) and is responsible for the transmission and distribution of natural gas in the southern region of Pakistan, covering the provinces of Sindh and Balochistan, where it enjoys a monopoly position. Under the Petroleum Exploration and Production Policy 2012, E&P companies are required to sell a major portion of their share of gas to GoP through its nominated buyer which is effectively controlled by it.  
This ‘per se’ suggests that there is no typical ‘dealer-distributor’ or ‘wholesaler’ arrangement of SSGC with UEPL. Even the onward sale by SSGC to end-consumers or decision to supply gas to ‘industrial’, 'residential' and ‘commercial’ areas in the region and the pricing at which such sale is to be made is regulated by GoP through OGRA. In other words, distribution of gas to end consumers is in effect in accordance with the decision of the GoP and, therefore, the common terms ‘wholesaler’/ ‘dealer’ / ‘distributor’ and ‘retailer’ itself when considered in terms of the extent of the operations of SSGC is, in our view, distinguishable and a case is made out for non-application of advance tax collection as per section 236G or 236H on the sales by UEPL. [Please confirm this fact as otherwise it would have significant bearing on the advice]
It is, nevertheless, important to understand the legislative intent and purpose behind the introduction of the above-mentioned sections in the Ordinance through Finance Bill 2013. To establish the same, we refer to the Salient features of the Finance Bill, 2013 wherein it was mentioned that contribution of the wholesale and retail sector towards the tax revenue does not commensurate with share of this sector in the GDP. To ensure documentation of the economy and to bring the traders into the tax net, all manufacturers were made liable to collect adjustable withholding tax from distributors, dealers, and wholesalers.
Considering the above, the legislative intent in the instant case appears to cover under its ambit the undocumented wholesale and retail sectors and not gas distribution companies like SSGC, being registered and documented sector. We further understand that the tax registrations of SSGC are also done under separate categories as gas distribution companies thus differentiating them from typical distributors, wholesalers and retailers and have been treated under the law as different from ordinary retailers / distributors / dealer / wholesaler etc. In case of SSGC, the sector is not only documented but regulated and there are licensing requirements as well. As such, SSGC is distinguishable from retailers / distributors / dealers / wholesaler etc.
Keeping the above in view, sections 236G and 236H should not apply to SSGC as they are already registered for tax purposes and already paying the taxes due upon them. UEPL while dealing with SSGC may take the above position. It is, however, cautioned that the tax department may not agree with the above interpretation and take a converse position to make out a case of non-compliance for UEPL, the chances of which, in our view, are not remote.
Owing to the above risk, we suggest that UEPL should obtain commercial indemnity from SSGC subject to the condition that SSGC will get its status clarified from the FBR within a specified timeframe in the context of sections 236G and 236H; alternatively, UEPL may opt to deduct tax under either of the two sections having higher tax rate.

The specific query for our consideration is whether advance tax under section 236G or 236H is required to be collected by UEPL from Sui Southern Gas Company Limited [SSGC], being the purchaser of Natural Gas.
SSGC is engaged in the transmission, distribution, and sale of gas in the franchise areas of Sindh and Baluchistan. As per the terms of the gas sale purchase agreement read with the relevant Petroleum Concession Agreements, the gas is offered to the President of Pakistan who has nominated SSGC to act on its behalf for the purchase of gas.
Section 236G mandates that "every manufacturer at the time of sale to distributors, dealers, and wholesalers shall collect advance tax." This is a requirement triggered only on sales made to these categories of persons and thus the relevant definitions need to be considered as to who qualifies as distributors, dealers, and wholesalers under the Ordinance.
Definition of “Distributor” under section 2(18A) of the Ordinance is: “Distributor means a person appointed by a manufacturer, importer or any other person for a specified area to purchase goods from him for further supply.”
There is requirement for a formal appointment by the manufacturer whereas between UEPL and SSGC there is no such arrangement. Sales terms are independent and non-obligatory and thus the UEPL’s sales case does not fall here.
Next, the terms ‘Dealers and Wholesalers’, which are not defined under the Ordinance.
Under legal terms: (source: Blacks’ law): “A dealer, in the popular, and therefore in the statutory, sense of the word, is not one who buys to keep, or makes to sell, but one who buys to sell again.”
(source: Merriams-Websters): “one that deals.”
Wholesale: To sell by wholesale, is to sell by large parcels, generally in original packages, and not by retail. 
Lastly, is the case of sale by SSGC to end consumers and any implication of Section 236H of the Ordinance. Section 236H mandates the collection of advance tax at the time of sale to retailers. This includes manufacturers, distributors, dealers, wholesalers, or commercial importers selling goods to entities classified as retailers. The section aims to ensure advance tax collection on sales made within the retail supply chain and retailers are specifically defined as entities engaged in selling goods to end consumers as part of their business operations.
A bare perusal of all the above definitions suggests that SSGC could come under the grab of both sections 236G and 236H. However, there are arguments to assert that neither section applies to SSGC:
SSGC is a licensed buyer of natural gas, specifically appointed/nominated by the President of Pakistan to purchase gas on its behalf. SSGC is a publicly listed company that operates under the administrative control of the Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) and is responsible for the transmission and distribution of natural gas in the southern region of Pakistan, covering the provinces of Sindh and Balochistan, where it enjoys a monopoly position. Under the Petroleum Exploration and Production Policy 2012, E&P companies are required to sell a major portion of their share of gas to GoP through its nominated buyer which is effectively controlled by it.  
This ‘per se’ suggests that there is no typical ‘dealer-distributor’ or ‘wholesaler’ arrangement of SSGC with UEPL. Even the onward sale by SSGC to end-consumers or decision to supply gas to ‘industrial’, 'residential' and ‘commercial’ areas in the region and the pricing at which such sale is to be made is regulated by GoP through OGRA. In other words, distribution of gas to end consumers is in effect in accordance with the decision of the GoP and, therefore, the common terms ‘wholesaler’/ ‘dealer’ / ‘distributor’ and ‘retailer’ itself when considered in terms of the extent of the operations of SSGC is, in our view, distinguishable and a case is made out for non-application of advance tax collection as per section 236G or 236H on the sales by UEPL. [Please confirm this fact as otherwise it would have significant bearing on the advice]
It is, nevertheless, important to understand the legislative intent and purpose behind the introduction of the above-mentioned sections in the Ordinance through Finance Bill 2013. To establish the same, we refer to the Salient features of the Finance Bill, 2013 wherein it was mentioned that contribution of the wholesale and retail sector towards the tax revenue does not commensurate with share of this sector in the GDP. To ensure documentation of the economy and to bring the traders into the tax net, all manufacturers were made liable to collect adjustable withholding tax from distributors, dealers, and wholesalers.
Considering the above, the legislative intent in the instant case appears to cover under its ambit the undocumented wholesale and retail sectors and not gas distribution companies like SSGC, being registered and documented sector. We further understand that the tax registrations of SSGC are also done under separate categories as gas distribution companies thus differentiating them from typical distributors, wholesalers and retailers and have been treated under the law as different from ordinary retailers / distributors / dealer / wholesaler etc. In case of SSGC, the sector is not only documented but regulated and there are licensing requirements as well. As such, SSGC is distinguishable from retailers / distributors / dealers / wholesaler etc.
Keeping the above in view, sections 236G and 236H should not apply to SSGC as they are already registered for tax purposes and already paying the taxes due upon them. UEPL while dealing with SSGC may take the above position. It is, however, cautioned that the tax department may not agree with the above interpretation and take a converse position to make out a case of non-compliance for UEPL, the chances of which, in our view, are not remote.
Owing to the above risk, we suggest that UEPL should obtain commercial indemnity from SSGC subject to the condition that SSGC will get its status clarified from the FBR within a specified timeframe in the context of sections 236G and 236H; alternatively, UEPL may opt to deduct tax under either of the two sections having higher tax rate.
