Hi Komal, 

This is with reference to your E-mail through which you have sought our views regarding applicability of Sindh Sales Tax on renting of immovable property in the wake of decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan dated September 5, 2022. 

It is to be noted that the said judgment of SC has confirmed the earlier decision of the Sindh High Court (SHC) in case of Young's (Private) Limited. Nevertheless, as you are already aware, to nullify the effect of the decision of SHC, the definition of “economic activity” provided in the section 4 of the Act was amended through the Sindh Sales Tax on Services (Amendment) Act, 2018 dated 11 April 2018 (with retrospective effect from 01 July 2015) which included renting of immovable property under the purview of economic activity. The earlier judgment of SHC held that renting of immovable property was neither a service nor taxable service or part of economic activity as defined.  The Supreme Court in its judgment (while confirming the judgment of SHC) held that:

"2. Learned counsel for the appellant argued that renting of immovable property per se is a "taxable service" under section 3 of the Act and, therefore, liable to sales tax on services under section 8 of the Act. We have examined the impugned judgment in detail. The High Court, after an elaborate discussion, held that a cumulative reading of sections 2(728), 2(72C), 3, 4, 5 and 8 of the Act shows that "taxable service" is that which is provided by a registered person in the course of an economic activity from his registered office or place of business in Sindh. What the appellants want to tax is not taxable service liable to taxation under the Act. The mere renting out of property by a landlord to a tenant is not taxable as it is not a taxable service.

3. The grounds raised by the appellants have been convincingly answered in the impugned judgment. We are in complete agreement with the learned Judges of the High Court and see no reason to take a view different from the one taken by the High Court in its well-reasoned judgment or the necessity to further elaborate on any aspect of the matter. The listed appeals are, therefore, dismissed."
(emphasis added)

3.	The SC has, as emphasised above, in the first part confirmed the view that mere renting of immovable property is not a taxable service. This first part of judgement may be argued as dependent upon un-amended definition of economic activity (which effectively form part of definition of taxable service). Therefore, to that extent it may be argued that the said part of the judgment may not be squarely applicable in the post-amended era.

4.	However, in the second part, as emphasised above, SC has shown complete agreement with the judgement of SHC, which had also held that renting of immovable property is not a “service”. This inference can be drawn and applicable even now as this interpretation is based on general connotation of the term “services”, still unaffected by any legislative amendment.

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing in response to your recent email seeking clarification on the applicability of Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on the renting of immovable property, particularly in light of the Supreme Court of Pakistan's decision dated September 5, 2022.

As mentioned in your email, the Supreme Court's ruling affirmed the Sindh High Court's (SHC) earlier decision in the case of Young's (Private) Limited. Notably, the SHC's decision was countered by an amendment to the definition of "economic activity" in Section 4 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services (Amendment) Act, 2018, effective from July 1, 2015. This amendment explicitly included renting of immovable property within the scope of economic activity.

The Supreme Court, while upholding the SHC's judgment, clarified that the mere renting out of property by a landlord to a tenant does not constitute a taxable service under the Act. The Court held that taxing such transactions was not warranted as they did not fall within the definition of taxable service.

Upon careful analysis of the Supreme Court's decision, it can be argued that the first part of the judgment, which negates the taxability of mere renting, may be influenced by the pre-amendment definition of economic activity. However, the second part of the judgment, where the Supreme Court aligns with the SHC's view that renting of immovable property is not a service, holds relevance even in the post-amendment era, as it is based on the general connotation of the term "services" unaffected by legislative changes.

In light of the above, we opine that the Supreme Court's decision remains applicable post the Amendment Act of 2018, suggesting that SST may not be applicable to renting of immovable property.

However, it is crucial to note that after the amendment in 2018, the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) asserted that SST is indeed applicable to renting of immovable property. In response, tenants and landlords challenged this assertion in the SHC and secured interim stay orders. 3.1	To substantiate the contention that assessment proceedings under section 122(9) of the Ordinance can only be initiated once the proceedings under section 111 are completed, it is imperative to analyse the legal framework, procedural requirements, and relevant judicial interpretations in conjunction with the specific circumstances of the instance case.

3.2	Section 111 of the Ordinance addresses the concealment of income. It empowers the Commissioner of Inland Revenue to issue a notice to a taxpayer if there is reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has been concealed, under-reported, or has escaped assessment. The key elements of Section 111 are:

•	Issuance of Notice: The Commissioner must issue a notice to the taxpayer, providing details of the suspected concealed income.

•	Response and Explanation: The taxpayer is required to furnish a response and explanation regarding the concealed income.

•	Formation of Opinion: Based on the response, the Commissioner must form an opinion on whether the income has been concealed or under-reported.

3.3	The proceedings under section 111 of the Ordinance are investigative and aim to establish the factual basis for any concealed income. Only after this investigative process is complete and the Commissioner forms a definitive opinion can the information be considered "definite."

3.4	Section 122(5) of the Ordinance allows the Commissioner to amend an assessment if there is "definite information" that income has escaped assessment, has been under-assessed, or has been subject to excessive relief or refund. The term "definite information" is critical here, as it must be concrete and substantiated. Section 122(9) of the Ordinance outlines the procedural requirements for amending an assessment. It mandates the issuance of a notice to the taxpayer, detailing the reasons for the proposed amendment, and provides the taxpayer with an opportunity to respond.

3.5	The Sequence and Dependency of Proceedings:

•	Completion of Section 111 Proceedings: The proceedings under section 111 of the Ordinance must be completed first. This includes the issuance of a notice, the taxpayer's response, and the formation of an opinion by the Commissioner. This step ensures that the Commissioner has a substantiated basis (definite information) for any amendments to the assessment.

•	Formation of Definite Information: The conclusion of section 111 of the Ordinance proceedings results in the formation of definite information. This information is essential for invoking section 122(5) of the Ordinance, as it provides the concrete evidence needed to justify any amendments to the tax assessment.

•	Initiation of Section 122(9) Proceedings: Only after the definite information is established through the completion of section 111 of the Ordinance proceedings can the Commissioner issue a notice under Section 122(9). This notice must detail the reasons for the proposed amendment based on the definite information obtained.

The protections under PERA have judicial endorsement, as seen in the case reported as 1998 PTD 34, decided by the Full Bench of the Lahore High Court. ### Jurisdiction and Legislative Authority Post-18th Amendment

Following the 18th Amendment to the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, the jurisdiction over labor-related matters has been devolved to the provinces. This constitutional amendment has significant implications for labor legislation and its enforcement across Pakistan's provinces, including Sindh, where our client's operations are predominantly based. 

### Provincial Jurisdiction Over Labor Matters

In light of this devolution, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) does not hold concurrent jurisdiction to enforce recovery of labor-related dues within Sindh. The authority now lies with the provincial government, specifically with the institutions established under the legislative framework of Sindh. This transition underscores the autonomy of provincial authorities in handling labor matters and underscores the provincial government's primacy in these areas.

### Sindh Companies Profits (Workers' Participation) Bill, 2015

The Sindh Companies Profits (Workers' Participation) Bill, 2015, represents a crucial piece of legislation in the context of workers' participation in company profits. Passed by the Provincial Assembly of Sindh on April 22, 2016, and assented to by the Governor of Sindh on May 16, 2016, this Act mandates companies operating within the province to allocate a portion of their profits to their workers. This legislative requirement underscores the commitment to enhancing workers' welfare and participation in corporate prosperity.

To our understanding, the GB Council has adopted the STA 1990 through the Sales Tax Act (Enforcement) Order 1999, which applies to the entirety of GB. Through this Enforcement Order, all provisions, notifications, circulars, and orders, including amendments to the Act, are deemed applicable in GB. Additionally, through a notification dated January 4, 2018, the Gilgit Baltistan Council suspended the recovery of income tax. However, we are not aware of any such notification issued for sales tax purposes.

Therefore, the question arises as to whether SPL would be obligated to levy sales tax under the GB adapted Sales Tax Act on supplies made within the territory of GB, where the title of goods is transferred within GB. In our interpretation, the answer is affirmative. This is due to the fact that SPL, by supplying taxable goods within GB, would transfer ownership of the goods to consumers in GB. If a Pakistani resident is remunerated salary income by a foreign company, the tax implications on the individual hinge on the location where the employment is exercised. Given that any salary received by a person working in Pakistan constitutes Pakistan-source income, the salary income would be taxable in Pakistan even if paid by a foreign company, as long as the employment is conducted in Pakistan.

For a Pakistani source income, such as salary, the tax liability remains regardless of whether the individual is a resident or non-resident. The taxation of salary income is contingent upon the physical exercise of employment. Therefore, if the employment is exercised in Pakistan, irrespective of residency status, the income becomes taxable in Pakistan, regardless of who disburses the salary.

In the scenario where an individual is a resident of Dubai but employed by UEP Pakistan Branch and performs duties from Pakistan, the taxation of salary income depends on the physical location of employment. If the individual is physically present in Pakistan, their salary income is taxable in Pakistan, even if working remotely for a Pakistan-based branch of a foreign company.

Regarding non-resident employees seconded to an associate company in another country and relocated, the taxation of salary income still depends on the physical location of employment. If the employment is exercised in Pakistan, the income is taxable in Pakistan, irrespective of where the payment originates.

Concerning salary-related payments in USD by a permanent establishment in Pakistan, generally, Pakistani companies are not permitted to pay salaries in foreign currency without approval from the State Bank of Pakistan. 4.2	Section 111 of the Ordinance addresses the concealment of income. It empowers the Commissioner of Inland Revenue to issue a notice to a taxpayer if there is reason to believe that any income chargeable to tax has been concealed, under-reported, or has escaped assessment. The key elements of Section 111 are:

•	Issuance of Notice: The Commissioner must issue a notice to the taxpayer, providing details of the suspected concealed income.

•	Response and Explanation: The taxpayer is required to furnish a response and explanation regarding the concealed income.

•	Formation of Opinion: Based on the response, the Commissioner must form an opinion on whether the income has been concealed or under-reported.

4.3	The proceedings under section 111 of the Ordinance are investigative and aim to establish the factual basis for any concealed income. Only after this investigative process is complete and the Commissioner forms a definitive opinion can the information be considered "definite."

4.4	Section 122(5) of the Ordinance allows the Commissioner to amend an assessment if there is "definite information" that income has escaped assessment, has been under-assessed, or has been subject to excessive relief or refund. The term "definite information" is critical here, as it must be concrete and substantiated. Section 122(9) of the Ordinance outlines the procedural requirements for amending an assessment. It mandates the issuance of a notice to the taxpayer, detailing the reasons for the proposed amendment, and provides the taxpayer with an opportunity to respond.

4.5	The Sequence and Dependency of Proceedings:

•	Completion of Section 111 Proceedings: The proceedings under section 111 of the Ordinance must be completed first. This includes the issuance of a notice, the taxpayer's response, and the formation of an opinion by the Commissioner. This step ensures that the Commissioner has a substantiated basis (definite information) for any amendments to the assessment.

•	Formation of Definite Information: The conclusion of section 111 of the Ordinance proceedings results in the formation of definite information. This information is essential for invoking section 122(5) of the Ordinance, as it provides the concrete evidence needed to justify any amendments to the tax assessment.

•	Initiation of Section 122(9) Proceedings: Only after the definite information is established through the completion of section 111 of the Ordinance proceedings can the Commissioner issue a notice under Section 122(9). This notice must detail the reasons for the proposed amendment based on the definite information obtained.

4.6	Coming back to the instant case, your good office had initiated proceedings under section 111 of the Ordinance by issuing a notice with barcode No. 100000197932670 dated June 11, 2024, with a compliance date set for June 17, 2024. Nevertheless, according to the General Clauses Act, if the compliance date falls within a Gazetted holiday, the compliance date is extended to the next working day. Given that the compliance date of June 17, 2024, fell during Eid Gazetted holidays, the due date for compliance extended to June 20, 2024.

4.7	Keeping in view of the above, your good office prematurely issued a notice under section 122(5A) read with Section 122(9) of the Ordinance before the extended compliance date, alleging non-submission of a response under section 111 of the Ordinance. This action is both procedurally incorrect and contrary to the principles upheld by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in recent judgment dated February 1, 2024 (a copy enclosed as Annexure ‘A’, for your perusal), which emphasize adherence to due process and fair trial standards. For the sake of brevity, the operating paragraphs of the said judgement are reproduced below: 

16	However, in order to clarify, even if the Explanation was applicable to the instant matters, the proceedings under Section 111 would still require to be taken up first and finalized before the proceedings under Section 122(5) can formally proceed. This is in line with the scheme of Section 111 and its effect on Section 122, as explained above. The effect of the Explanation, therefore, is only to dispense with the requirement of a separate notice under Section 111, however, it cannot subsume two different and distinguishable proceedings under Section 111 and 122. As such, while the Explanation dispenses with the requirement of a separate notice under Section 111, it does not dispense with the requirement that in case proceedings are initiated under Section 122(5) on the basis of definite information to be provided through Section 111, the proceedings under Section 111 are to be concluded first in the manner provided under the law and till such time, the proceedings under Section 122(9) cannot be given effect to.

17	Therefore, where one notice is issued under Section 122(9) which encompasses both the grounds of Section 111(1) and Section 122(5), the proceedings under Section 111 will be taken up first. However, where the response is not satisfactory, the Commissioner will then form an opinion, as is required under Section 111, which can only be taken as definite information for the purposes of Section 122(5) for amendment of the assessment. ### Contention: Addition under Section 111 Cannot Be Made Without an Inquiry, Which is Beyond the Scope of Section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance

In the case of Atif Aslam v. CIR Legal, RTO Lahore, the appellate tribunal has provided significant insights into the limitations and procedural requirements associated with the invocation of Section 111 and Section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

#### Background

The case revolves around the addition of income under Section 111 of the Ordinance, which deals with unexplained income or assets. The appellant, Mr. Atif Aslam, challenged the remand of the addition made under Section 111 by the learned appellate authority. The appellant argued that the manner in which Section 111 was invoked was procedurally flawed and beyond the jurisdictional scope provided by Section 122(5A).

#### Legal Arguments

1. **Sequence and Procedural Requirements**:
   - The appellate representative (AR) for the taxpayer contended that as per the principles established by the Honourable Apex Court in the case reported as 2021 PTD 1182, a notice under Section 111 must be issued either prior to or simultaneously with the notice under Section 122. This is because proceedings under Section 111 should culminate in an appropriate order, providing "definite information" that justifies an amendment under Section 122.
   - The tribunal emphasized that issuing a notice under Section 122 prior to completing the proceedings under Section 111 is unlawful and without jurisdiction. This procedural misstep was evident in the appellant’s case, rendering the subsequent actions of the tax authorities invalid.

2. **Scope of Section 122(5A)**:
   - Section 122(5A) pertains to the amendment of assessments in specific situations, primarily when there is definite information available that indicates that income has escaped assessment. However, the tribunal clarified that definite information resulting from proceedings under Section 111 should ideally lead to amendments under Section 122(5), not Section 122(5A). This is because Section 122(5) is more aligned with the nature of definite information about concealed income.
   - The tribunal referred to previous judgments, such as ITA No. 1064/KB/2015 and 108 TAX 35, which support the stance that any addition under Section 111 requires a thorough inquiry, something that falls outside the purview of Section 122(5A).

3. **Time Limitations and Legal Precedents**:
   - The AR also highlighted that the tax authorities' demand for records beyond the time limitation specified under Section 174 of the Ordinance was without lawful authority. The Honourable Apex Court's ruling in Civil Petition No. 1691-L of 2018 reaffirmed that taxpayers cannot be compelled to produce records for periods exceeding the statutory limit.
   - This contention further undermines the validity of the tax authorities’ actions, as they demanded records for periods outside the permissible timeframe, violating the taxpayer's rights and established legal precedents.

#### Conclusion

The tribunal annulled the orders of the authorities below, siding with the taxpayer’s contentions. It was firmly established that any addition under Section 111 must be preceded by a proper inquiry and issuance of notice in accordance with procedural requirements. Moreover, such an addition should lead to proceedings under Section 122(5), not Section 122(5A), ensuring adherence to the legal framework and protection of taxpayer rights. ### Contention: Addition under Section 111 Cannot Be Made Without an Inquiry, Which is Beyond the Scope of Section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance

In the case of Atif Aslam v. CIR Legal, RTO Lahore (ITA No. 271/LB/2021), the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue Lahore Bench has provided critical insights into the procedural and jurisdictional limitations associated with invoking Section 111 and Section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

#### Background

The appellant, Mr. Atif Aslam, a renowned artist deriving income from singing and allied artistic pursuits, challenged the remand order issued by the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals-VII), Lahore, which had annulled and remanded the addition made under Section 111 of the Ordinance. The appeal focused on the procedural irregularities and jurisdictional overreach by the tax authorities in invoking Section 111 after issuing a notice under Section 122.

#### Legal Framework

1. **Section 111 of the Ordinance**:
   - Section 111 addresses the taxation of unexplained income or assets and mandates a detailed inquiry to establish definite information regarding such unexplained amounts.
   - According to the principles established by the Honourable Apex Court, proceedings under Section 111 must culminate in an appropriate order, which then serves as the definite information required for amending assessments under Section 122.

2. **Section 122(5A) of the Ordinance**:
   - Section 122(5A) deals with the amendment of assessments when there is definite information that income has escaped assessment.
   - The Honourable Apex Court has clarified that amendments based on definite information from Section 111 proceedings should be conducted under Section 122(5), not Section 122(5A), due to the different scopes and purposes of these sections.

#### Key Contentions and Tribunal Findings

1. **Sequence and Procedural Requirements**:
   - The appellant's representative argued that the notice under Section 111 should either precede or coincide with the notice under Section 122 to ensure procedural compliance and lawful invocation of jurisdiction.
   - The Tribunal referenced the Apex Court's judgment in 2021 PTD 1182, which established that initiating proceedings under Section 122 before concluding Section 111 inquiries is unlawful. The Court emphasized that definite information required under Section 122 must emerge from concluded proceedings under Section 111.

2. **Jurisdictional Overreach**:
   - The Tribunal noted that the notice under Section 122 was issued prior to the notice under Section 111 in the appellant's case. This procedural misstep invalidates the subsequent actions of the tax authorities, as the initial notice under Section 122 was premature and lacked the requisite definite information.
   - The Tribunal emphasized that the proper legal course involves concluding inquiries under Section 111 first, which should then provide the definite information necessary for any amendment under Section 122(5), not Section 122(5A).

3. **Adherence to Time Limitations**:
   - The appellant’s representative highlighted that the tax authorities' demand for records extending beyond the statutory time limit under Section 174(3) was unlawful. The Honourable Apex Court has consistently ruled that taxpayers cannot be compelled to produce records beyond the legally prescribed period.
   - The Tribunal affirmed that such demands violate taxpayer rights and contravene established legal precedents, further undermining the validity of the tax authorities' actions in this case.

4. **Prior Judicial Precedents**:
   - The Tribunal referenced previous rulings, such as ITA No. 1064/KB/2015 and 108 TAX 35, which support the position that any addition under Section 111 necessitates a thorough inquiry that is beyond the scope of Section 122(5A).
   - These rulings reinforce the necessity for proper procedural conduct and jurisdictional adherence when invoking Sections 111 and 122.

#### Conclusion

The Tribunal concluded that the tax authorities' actions in this case were procedurally flawed and beyond their jurisdiction. The notice under Section 122 issued prior to completing proceedings under Section 111 invalidated the subsequent addition. Furthermore, the Tribunal underscored that any addition under Section 111 requires a detailed inquiry, and the resultant definite information should lead to amendments under Section 122(5), not Section 122(5A).

The appeal was thus allowed, and the orders of the lower authorities were annulled. This decision reaffirms the importance of adhering to due process and respecting taxpayer rights, ensuring that tax administration is conducted fairly and transparently in accordance with the law.

**Detailed Summary:**

The dispute in the petroleum sector revolves around the imposition of the super tax, with key representatives including Nasim Sikandar, Jamal Sukhera, Mansoor Awan, and Zainab Janjua. They argue against the tax, primarily relying on the Regulation of Mines and Oil-Fields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948 (the 1948 Act). Specifically, Sections 3B and 4 of the 1948 Act provide concessions to petroleum exploration companies, and the Schedule to the Act outlines conditions related to amendments in the Income Tax Ordinance 1979 after the effective date of a Petroleum Concession Agreement (PCA).

The crux of their argument is grounded in the freezing clause found in all PCAs, stating that the taxation liability is fixed on the date the PCA is signed. This assurance, they contend, was a pivotal factor influencing petroleum investors to commit their investments. They claim that any taxation exceeding what was agreed upon at the time of signing violates the statutory provisions of the 1948 Act.

Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule further reinforces the position that taxes should not exceed the limits set in the PCAs. However, the introduction of the super tax under Section 4C by the Finance Act 2022 complicates matters. The petitioners argue that the super tax wasn't part of their original PCA agreements and, when factoring in this new tax, their aggregate liability surpasses the caps stipulated in Rule 4.

The argument also delves into the Ocean Pakistan case, emphasizing that its judgment, which suggested the Ordinance could override the 1948 Act, is currently suspended by the Supreme Court. The petitioners contend that the Ocean Pakistan case was based on an erroneous assumption and is not applicable to their situation.

Additionally, the legal analysis explores the intricacies of relevant clauses, including the freezing clause, in the PCAs and the legislative framework. It scrutinizes whether the new tax is compatible with the existing agreements and whether the special provisions for the petroleum sector under the 1948 Act take precedence over general tax laws.

In essence, the dispute hinges on whether the imposition of the super tax, not originally contemplated in the PCAs, breaches the frozen tax liabilities agreed upon in those contracts, as protected by the 1948 Act. The analysis also highlights the complexities arising from the interplay between specific and general tax laws and the potential impact on investors in the petroleum sector.

Petroleum sector-specific submissions against the imposition of super tax were led primarily by Messrs Nasim Sikandar, Jamal Sukhera, Mansoor Awan, and Ms Zainab Janjua, representing petroleum exploration and production companies, resting their case on the Regulation of Mines and Oil-Fields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948 (the 1948 Act) and, in case of Spud Energy (Private) Limited, on 100 of the Ordinance read with Part 1 of the Fifth Schedule.
Sections 3B and 4 of the 1948 Act in so far as material are reproduced below: 
3B. Concessions to petroleum exploration companies.__ 
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, every company … to whom a licence or a lease to explore, prospect and mine petroleum is granted under this Act… shall be entitled to the concessions specified in the Schedule... 
4. Effect of rules etc., inconsistent with other enactments. 
Any rule made under this Act, and any order made under any such rule, shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment or in any instrument having effect by virtue of an enactment other than this Act. 
Part I of the Schedule to the 1948 Act referred to in section 3B in material part reads as follows: 
… any amendment in the Income Tax Ordinance 1979… made after the effective date of an agreement for the grant of a licence or lease to explore, prospect or mine petroleum, which are inconsistent with the terms of the agreement, shall not apply to the extent of such inconsistency to a company which is a party to the agreement.
Clause 2 of the Schedule in material part reads as follows: 
…taxes on income shall be fixed at the time of grant of the permit or licence…
The contention therefore is that on the date a Petroleum Concession Agreement (PCA) is signed, the law on taxation including the rates of tax are frozen in respect of the income that may be derived by exploiting the concession which is the subject of that PCA. This pact between the President of Pakistan as the grantor of the concession and the concessionaire company is termed as „the freezing clause‟, which is found in all PCAs. Mr. Sikandar referred to Article 12 titled “Taxation” of his client’s PCA, calling it a standard provision in all PCAs, and this has not been denied by Ms. Hamid. Clauses 12.1, 12.4 and 12.7 of the PCA have the cumulative effect that the provisions of Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 in force on the date the PCA was signed were to apply for the taxation limiting the tax exposure to „… fifty-five percent (55%) of profits or gains derived from the operations …‟ but in case of a conflict between the provisions of the PCA „…and the provisions now in effect of the Ordinance, and the Fifth Schedule thereof…‟ the latter was to prevail. Clause 20.2 is the primary freezing clause and stipulates that the Income Tax Ordinance 1979 as in force on the date of PCA was to apply regardless of any subsequent amendments thereto.
The crux of the petitioners‟ arguments is that the taxation liability was frozen on the date the PCAs were signed and that it was on the basis of that certainty as to the exposure to taxation that the petroleum investors decided to come forward to sign the PCAs and commit their investment. Any taxation that exceeded that tax exposure violated the statutory command under sections 3B and 4 of the 1948 Act read with Clauses 1 and 2 of the Schedule thereto read with the freezing clause of the PCA. This argument is simple and forceful and prevails with me, but necessitates a discussion on the judgment of the Division Bench of this Court in Ocean Pakistan54 , which remained the mainstay of Ms. Hamid‟s submissions in reply. Mr. Mansoor Awan and Ms. Zainab Janjua for Spud Energy made additional submissions specific to their clients.
One provision of law cannot make the other redundant or nugatory without an express intention and expression to that end, which is to be spelt out, as is the convention in legislative drafting, by inserting a non-obstante clause, but which is conspicuous by its absence in § 4C. On the contrary, the non-obstante clause appears in section 3B of the 1948 Act, although it is conditioned by reference to any other law for the time being in force, and the Schedule to the 1948 Act by its language makes the concessions stipulated in a PCA on its effective date operative for the future as well by expressly excluding the application of „any amendment in the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979‟ after the effective date of the PCA to the extent such amendment is inconsistent with the terms of the PCA.
While repealing the ITO 1979, the Ordinance vide §100 stipulated the taxation of E&P companies in accordance with the Fifth Schedule of the Ordinance. Section 100 is the charging section for E&P companies. By virtue of §8 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, references in a legislation to another legislation are to be read as references to the successor legislation to that other legislation, and therefore the references to ITO 1979 in the 1948 Act are to be read as references to the Ordinance replacing the ITO 1979. 
The submissions at the bar did not go into any depth in the differences between the Fifth Schedule to the Ordinance and the Fifth Schedule to the ITO 1979, and remained confined to a general statement that no tax could be imposed that did not exist at the time the PCA was signed. Clause 2(6) of the Fifth Schedule permits carry forward of deductions under Part IV of Chapter III. Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule is directly in point for the argument under consideration and is reproduced in material part below:-
4. Limitation on Payment to Federal Government and Taxes 
(1) The aggregate of the taxes on income and other payments …on, or after, the first day of July 2001 to the Government in respect of the profits or gains derived from such undertaking for a tax year shall not exceed the limits provided for in the agreement, provided the said aggregate shall not be less than fifty per cent of the profits or gains derived by an onshore petroleum exploration and production undertaking and forty per cent of the profits or gains derived by an offshore petroleum exploration and production undertaking, before deduction of the payment to the Federal Government. 
… 
(3) If, in respect of any tax year, the aggregate of the taxes on income and payments to the Federal Government is greater or less than the amount provided for in the agreement, an additional amount of tax shall be payable by the taxpayer, or an abatement of tax shall be allowed to the taxpayer, as the case may be, so as to make the aggregate of the taxes on income and payments to the Federal Government equal to the amount provided for in the agreement. 
(4) If, in respect of any year, the payments to the Federal Government exceed the amount provided for in the agreement, so much of the excess as consists of any tax or levy referred to in subclause (b) of clause (3) of rule 6 shall be carried forward and treated, for the purposes of this rule, as payments to the Federal Government for the succeeding year, provided that the whole of the Writ Petition no.4027 of 2022 -32- payments to the Federal Government exceeding the amount provided for in such agreement may be carried forward if so provided for in any agreement with a taxpayer made before the first day of 1970. 
(4A) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Schedule, a person, for tax year 2012 and onward, may opt to pay tax at the rate of forty per cent of the profits and gains, net of royalty, derived by a petroleum exploration and production undertaking. 
… 
4AB. The provisions of section 4C shall apply to the taxpayers under this schedule and shall be taxed at the rates specified in Division IIB of Part I of the First Schedule from tax year 2022 onwards.
Rule 4(1) of the Fifth Schedule stipulated that the aggregate of the taxes on income and other payments were not to exceed the limits provided for in the PCAs, but were not to be less than 40% of the profits or gain of the onshore E&P company. The repeat references in all the sub-rules of Rule 4 to the taxation remaining at par with the amount stipulated in the PCA is an endorsement of § 3-B and 4 of the 1948 Act, in that the limitation on taxes is conditioned by the amount or the cap stipulated in the PCAs. Ms. Hamid‟s submission with reference to Rule 4(4) that any taxes imposed under the Ordinance leading to an excess over and above the cap provided in the PCA were to be carried forward and to be treated as payment of tax to the Federal Government for the next year is incorrect. In fact, this stipulation is only in respect of sub-clause (b) of clause 3 of Rule 6, which is confined to any tax “…peculiarly applicable to oil production… and not generally imposed upon all industrial and commercial activities”. The intent is quite obvious, that a general taxation measure applicable to all companies was not to apply to petroleum companies for the reason of 3B and 4 of the 1948 Act read with Rules 4(1),(2) and (3) freezing the taxation liability as of the date of the PCA, and it was only in respect of taxation specific to petroleum companies that a carry forward of excess tax was stipulated as a concession specific to petroleum sector specific taxation. 
This brings us to insertion of Rule 4AB in the Fifth Schedule reproduced above. The Finance Act imposed a new tax, the super tax under 4C, which to the extent of E&P petitioners was not catered for in their PCAs. However, it has not been pleaded before this Court whether the taxability to super tax increased their aggregate liability under taxes and other payments payable to the Federal Government above the caps stipulated in Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule. That is a matter for computation to be carried out in respect of each E&P company and, to the extent the cap is exceeded, the super tax for such E&P companies cannot be charged by virtue of the protection conferred on them under the PCAs, read with 3B and 4 of the 1948 Act.
Turning now to Ocean Pakistan case, the judgment therein stands suspended by the Supreme Court55. Further, to the extent it turned on the argument that the Ordinance was a special law and the 1948 Act was a general law, in my respectful view, it is actually the other way round. The 1948 Act was a special law in so far as it provided for taxation of a special subject, being the taxation of petroleum exploration companies. The Ordinance is a general law on income tax which applies to all persons liable to tax. But the special sub-class of taxpayers comprising the E&P companies is addressed under the 1948 Act, make the latter a special law on the subject. Further still, the relevant question of law in Ocean Pakistan was “Whether the ACIR erred in applying the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 instead of Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 as stipulated and guaranteed under the Petroleum Concession Agreement?”. In paragraph 15 of the judgement, the Court decided the said question by stating that “In such an eventuality, the provisions of the Ordinance of 1979 or Article 29.6 of the PCA are neither relevant nor attracted.” Having reached the aforesaid conclusion, the Court proceeded on an assumption to decide a larger question of whether section 54 of the 2001 Ordinance overrode section 3B of the 1948 Act. The said question was not referred to the Court and its observations from paragraph 16-23 were mere dicta.

Exporting IT and IT-enabled services has become an integral part of the country’s exports. The IT exports of Pakistan for the fiscal year 2021-22 were estimated to be around USD 3.5 billion, which is 66% higher than the fiscal year 2020-21, and is estimated to reach USD 5 billion in the fiscal year 2022-23. A significant part of IT exports comprises IT services and IT-enabled services which are generally exported by freelancers.
Freelancing has now become one of the most common means of IT Exports in Pakistan, and due to the Covid-19 pandemic, its volume has increased drastically over the last few years. Pakistan currently ranks 4th among the world’s fastest-growing freelance markets and it significantly impacts Pakistan’s economy.
Before March 2021, the export of IT services and IT-enabled services/ Income of freelancers was exempt from tax with the condition that eighty percent (80%) of the export proceeds are remitted through normal banking channels to Pakistan as foreign exchange.
On March 22, 2021, the Government of Pakistan issued Tax laws (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 2021, in which tax exemption was withdrawn from the export of IT services and IT-enabled services and introduced 100% tax credits on the export of IT services and IT-enabled services subject to the fulfillment of some conditions for proper documentation of the economy and freelancers.
In the Finance Act 2022, effective from July 01, 2022, the clause for a 100% tax credit was omitted, making freelancers and IT service exporters liable to pay taxes.

The benchmark rate is defined as 5%, with an additional 1% for every successive tax year post-tax year 2001. This means the benchmark rate for tax year 2012 is 15%, and it increases by 1% each subsequent tax year. However, the Finance Act of 2012 has imposed an upper limit on the benchmark rate, capping it at a maximum of 10 percent.

This figure was then compared against the taxpayer's reported profit on bank accounts of Rs. 9,815,000, leading to a perceived shortfall of Rs. 4,009,790.

2. **Application of Correct Tax Rate**: Upon review, it is acknowledged that the tax rate of 10% used in the department’s calculation was not in alignment with the statutory provisions applicable during the relevant tax year. Specifically, as per Division IA of Part III of the First Schedule to the Ordinance, the correct tax rate for profit on bank accounts for the tax year in question was 15%, a rate that was subsequently amended by the Finance Act, 2019.

This recalculated figure is, in fact, lower than the amount of Rs. 9,815,000 reported by the taxpayer in their financial statements as profit on bank accounts. This indicates that the taxpayer has not underreported their interest income, but rather declared an amount in excess of the calculated figure based on the correct tax rate.

### Tajir Dost Scheme: How to Register & Calculate Tax

The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has introduced a new feature in its Tax Asaan app called the Tajir Dost Scheme, aimed at encouraging unregistered businesses to declare their assets and income by offering them certain benefits.

#### What is the Tajir Dost Scheme?
The Tajir Dost Scheme is a voluntary tax compliance program designed to help unregistered businesses join the tax system. By participating, businesses can declare their assets and income, potentially enjoying benefits like reduced tax rates and simplified compliance procedures.

#### How to Register for the Tajir Dost Scheme
To register for the Tajir Dost Scheme, follow these simple steps:
1. Download the Tax Asaan app from Google Play Store or Apple App Store.
2. Open the app and find the “Tajir Dost Scheme” option.
3. Follow the on-screen instructions, which may include entering your ID card number, mobile number, and other required details.
4. Submit the registration form.

#### Who is Eligible for the Tajir Dost Scheme?
While the exact eligibility criteria are still under development, the scheme likely targets unregistered businesses, particularly in sectors such as:
- Retail stores
- Wholesalers
- Service providers

#### Compulsory Registration Cities
Businesses in the following cities must register under the Tajir Dost Scheme:
Abbottabad, Attock, Bahawalnagar, Bahawalpur, Chakwal, Dera Ismail Khan, DG Khan, Faisalabad, Ghotki, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Gwadar, Hafizabad, Haripur, Hyderabad, Islamabad, Jhang, Jhelum, Karachi, Kasur, Khushab, Lahore, Larkana, Lasbela, Lodhran, Mandi Bahauddin, Mansehra, Mardan, Mirpurkhas, Multan, Nankana, Narowal, Peshawar, Quetta, Rahim Yar Khan, Rawalpindi, Sahiwal, Sarghoda, Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Sukkur, and Toba Tek Singh.

#### How to Calculate Tax under the Tajir Dost Scheme
The Tajir Dost Scheme uses an indicative income-based method for calculating tax, meaning your tax liability is estimated based on your business area rather than detailed financial records.

#### How to Pay Tax under the Tajir Dost Scheme
1. **Access the Tajir Dost Portal:** Log in to the Iris portal and click on the “Tajir Dost” icon.
2. **Enter Business Details:** Input your business area, and the system will automatically retrieve your business information.
3. **Calculate Annual Liability:** The portal will calculate your annual tax liability based on the provided information.
4. **Generate Payment Slip:** Click on the “Create PSID” icon to generate a Payment Slip ID (PSID).
5. **Make Payment:** Use the PSID to pay your monthly tax installment online or at a bank branch.

Key Points:
- **Equal Installments:** Your annual tax liability is divided into 12 monthly payments.
- **Auto-Calculation:** The system calculates your tax based on your business area.
- **Flexible Payment Options:** Pay online or at a bank branch.

#### Tax Slabs and Rates under the Tajir Dost Scheme
Here’s a quick overview of the tax rates:

| **Indicative Income** | **Annual Tax** | **Monthly Tax** |
|------------------------|---------------|----------------|
| Up to Rs. 600,000      | Rs. 1,200     | Rs. 100        |
| Rs. 680,000            | Rs. 12,000    | Rs. 1,000      |
| Up to Rs. 1,000,000    | Rs. 60,000    | Rs. 5,000      |
| Rs. 1,350,000          | Rs. 120,000   | Rs. 10,000     |
| Rs. 1,833,333          | Rs. 240,000   | Rs. 20,000     |

Additionally, small shop owners (e.g., those with shops up to 50 square feet) are liable for a fixed advance tax of Rs. 1,200 annually (Rs. 100 per month).

#### Key Changes Introduced
- **Expanded Definition of “Person”:** Now includes a broader range of business entities.
- **Expanded Definition of “Physical Place”:** Includes offices, homes, or any location linked to business operations.
- **Indicative Income:** The concept of estimated income based on factors like property value and location.

#### Non-Registration Consequences
If you don't register by the deadline, the FBR will enforce mandatory registration based on available information. Field officers may visit and confirm compulsory registration.

#### Who is Exempt from Registration?
- Companies
- National and international chains
- Businesses with multiple outlets
- Specific exclusions set by the FBR

#### Conclusion

Your good office has also referred to a judgement of the Honorable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue reported as 2000 PTD (Trib.) 3776.

3.2	In this respect, we would apprise your good office that the judgment referenced in your notice pertains to the treatment of receipts from Dividend Income under section 80D of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979. Nevertheless, the issue raised by your office concerns the charging of minimum tax under section 113 of the Ordinance on profit on debt. Furthermore, the Honorable Appellate Tribunal, in its decision, specified that the matter of the chargeability of interest on deposits under section 80D(2) was not under its purview. For your convenience, we have included paragraph 38 of the aforementioned decision for reference.

“38.	Consequently decision of the Division Bench of the Tribunal in I.T.As. Nos. 1220 and 1221/KB of 1998-99, dated 20-5-1999 is overruled and the decision in I.T.A. No.955/KB of 1998-99, dated 20-3-1999 is approved. (emphasis is ours)


3.3	As a result, we find that the interpretation offered by your good office concerning the imposition of minimum tax under section 113 of the Ordinance, as gleaned from the aforementioned reported decision, lacks relevance. Accordingly, we respectfully urge your office not to draw any adverse inferences based on this interpretation.

3.4	Without prejudice to the above, we would apprise your good office that the term turnover is defined in section 113 of the Ordinance as:

“In this section, “turnover” means –

(a)	The gross receipts, exclusive of sales tax and federal excise duty or any trade discounts shown on invoices or bills, derived from the sale of goods, and also excluding any amount taken as deemed income and is assessed as final discharge of the tax liability for which tax is already paid or payable;

(b)	the gross fees for the rendering of services for giving benefits including commissions; except covered by final discharge of tax liability for which tax is separately paid or payable;

(c)	the gross receipts from the execution of contracts; except covered by final discharge of tax liability for which tax is separately paid or payable; and

(d)	The company’s share of the amounts stated above of any association of persons of which the company is a member.”


3.5	It is clearly laid down that ‘turnover’ for the purposes of section 113 of the Ordinance must be used in the context stated in the law and not in accounting, commercial or general parlance. If such concepts were required/intended to be used, then there was no need for specific application and ‘only’ the term ‘turnover’ would have sufficed. The minimum tax is payable only on turnover representing:

-	supply of goods;
-	rendering, giving or supplying services or benefits; and
-	execution of contract


3.6	In addition to the above, the business of our client is primarily engaged in the manufacture and sale of tiles and trading of allied building products and any other receipt not forming part of the business income cannot be included in the determination of the amount of turnover. It is abundantly clear that profit on bank deposits, as stated do not fall within the ambit of any of terms referred above, therefore, minimum tax under section 113 of the Ordinance is not applicable on receipt in these forms. In this connection, it has also to be noted that the terms ‘Turnover’ and ‘Receipts’ are not synonymous. Even if such receipts are taken to be turnover, it is not included in the term ‘turnover’ in the explanation to section 113 of the Ordinance.

3.7	Further, an important aspect to consider is that the definition of ‘turnover’ is an exhaustive definition as the word ‘means’ has been used. If it would have been an inclusive definition with the words includes then there could have been a possibility for the enlargement of scope to include other amounts for this purpose. As stated earlier, the definition is restricted and cannot be extended in any manner outside the parameters laid down in that section. 

3.8	From perusal of the above definition, it is quite evident that the turnover includes gross receipts from sale of goods and thereby does not include receipts to the company from any other source including profit on debt.

3.9	In the light of the above submission, it is stated that the income from profit on debt should not be included in turnover for the purpose of levying minimum tax as the said receipts are not made to earn profit.

ByMah NoorAugust 1, 20241 Commenton How to Register & Calculate Tax for Tajir Dost Scheme
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has introduced a new option in its  Tax Asaan  app for the Tajir Dost Scheme. The scheme aims to bring unregistered businesses into the tax net and encourage them to declare their assets and income.
What is the Tajir Dost Scheme?
The Tajir Dost Scheme is a voluntary tax compliance scheme that offers benefits to unregistered businesses. Under the scheme, businesses can declare their assets and income and potentially receive benefits like reduced tax rates and simplified tax compliance procedures.
How to register for the Tajir Dost Scheme?
The exact registration process for the Tajir Dost Scheme may still be under development. However, based on the information provided, here’s a possible scenario:
1.	Download the Tax Asaan app from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store.
2.	Open the app and look for the “Tajir Dost Scheme” option (the option might be newly added).
3.	If available, follow the on-screen instructions to register. This may involve entering your ID card number, mobile number, and other required information.
4.	Submit the registration form.
Who are Eligible for the Tajir Dost Scheme?
The eligibility criteria for the Tajir Dost Scheme haven’t been officially confirmed. However, the scheme likely targets unregistered businesses, particularly those in specific sectors like:
•	Retail stores
•	Wholesalers
•	Service providers

How to Calculate Tax under Tajir Dost Scheme?
S.R.O. 1064 (I)/2024 is an amendment to the Tajir Dost Special Procedure, 2024, introduced through the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. This amendment aims to clarify and expand the scope of the original procedure.
How to Pay Tax under Tajir Dost Scheme?
Process Overview
1.	Access Tajir Dost: Locate and click on the “Tajir Dost” icon on the Iris portal (After logging into Iris).
2.	Provide Business Details: You’ll be asked to input your business area. The system will automatically retrieve your business information.
3.	Calculate Annual Liability: Based on your business area, the portal will calculate your annual tax liability.
4.	Generate Payment Slip: Click on the “Create PSID” icon to generate a unique Payment Slip ID (PSID).
5.	Make Payment: Use the generated PSID to pay your monthly tax installment through online banking or at a bank branch.
Key Points
•	Equal Installments: The total annual tax liability is divided into 12 equal monthly installments.
•	Auto-Calculation: The system automatically calculates your annual tax liability based on your business area.
•	Online and Offline Payment: You have the flexibility to pay through online banking or at a bank branch.
Indicative Income Tax Calculation Under Tajir Dost Scheme:
The Tajir Dost scheme employs an indicative income-based tax calculation method. This means that the tax liability is determined based on an estimated income rather than detailed financial records.
Tax Slabs and Rates of Tajir Dost Scheme:
The following table outlines the indicative income slabs and corresponding annual and monthly tax amounts:

Key Changes Introduced:
•	Definition of Person: The term “person” has been expanded to include a wider range of business entities such as wholesalers, dealers, distributors, retailers, manufacturers, importers, and those combining multiple business activities.

Hi Zeeshan,

I trust this message finds you well.

Thank you for your email seeking our views on the tax withholding implications related to the payment of SAP Annual License and Maintenance services to Beijing. The receiving entity is a resident of China, and Pakistan has a Double Tax Treaty (DTT) with China.

Before providing specific comments, we kindly request a detailed understanding of the transaction and the arrangement's substance. Additionally, could you please confirm whether the payment is being made to a service provider or a group company?

Regarding your query on the withholding tax implications at the time of remitting payment in China, we believe that, under Article III of the Pakistan-China DTT, the payment is not liable to tax in Pakistan. This is considering it falls under foreign source industrial or commercial profits of a non-resident without a Permanent Establishment in Pakistan. However, it is crucial to obtain an exemption certificate under section 152(5) of the Income Tax Ordinance before proceeding with payment without tax deduction. While some view the application for an exemption certificate as not mandatory, it may carry risks and face potential challenges by the Tax Department.

It is worth noting that the Tax Department may attempt to classify the payment as royalty. Our position is that payments for the acquisition of a software license or related services are not royalty if the rights granted by the software developer do not include commercial exploitation or monetization of the software. In the absence of such rights, the payment is considered a limited license for the company's internal use only. However, the Tax Department may argue otherwise and could potentially treat the services as "Fee for Offshore Digital Services," applying a 5% tax rate.

Concerning sales tax implications, we believe these services fall within the service tariff headings (i) 9838.000 – Intellectual Property services (taxable at 10% without input tax adjustment or may opt for 13% standard rate with input tax adjustment) or (ii) 9815.6000 – Software or IT-based system development consultants (taxable at 13%). For a non-resident entity, sales tax is applicable under the reverse charge mechanism (RCM). The company may contest this levy under RCM based on constitutional arguments.

We hope this provides the information you need. If you require further clarification or additional details, please feel free to reach out.

Hi Zeeshan,

I trust this message finds you well.

Thank you for reaching out and seeking our views on the tax implications related to the payment of SAP Annual License and Maintenance services to Beijing, considering the Double Tax Treaty (DTT) between Pakistan and China.

Before providing specific comments, we request a comprehensive understanding of the transaction and the arrangement's substance. Additionally, could you please confirm whether the payment is intended for a service provider or a group company?

On your query regarding withholding tax implications at the time of remitting payment in China, our earlier stance, based on a High Court Order, held that these payments fall under Article III of the Pakistan-China DTT. This position meant that the payment is not subject to tax in Pakistan, as it is considered foreign-source industrial or commercial profits of a non-resident without a Permanent Establishment in Pakistan.

However, it is crucial to note that the Supreme Court of Pakistan (SCP) recently overturned a sixteen-year-old decision of the High Court. The SCP ruled that receipts from the leasing of FLIC Software computer programs in Pakistan constitute royalty income under Article 12 of the Treaty. The decision stems from a case involving a company based in the Netherlands with no business presence in Pakistan. The SCP upheld the Income Tax Officer's treatment of the receipts as royalty and subjected them to a 15% income tax rate.

In light of the SCP decision, payments to a non-resident entity for similar services fall within the domain of Royalty. Consequently, UEP Pakistan Branch is required to withhold income tax at a rate of 12.5%, as per the DTT between Pakistan and China.

Regarding sales tax implications, we believe these services fall within the service tariff headings (i) 9838.000 – Intellectual Property services (taxable at 10% without input tax adjustment or may opt for 13% standard rate with input tax adjustment) or (ii) 9815.6000 – Software or IT-based system development consultants (taxable at 13%). For a non-resident entity, sales tax is applicable under the reverse charge mechanism (RCM). The company may contest this levy under RCM based on constitutional arguments.

The AR explained that the said difference alleged by the ACIR through the impugned order is due to timing difference. It's essential to understand that the revenue figures disclosed in the Audited Financial Statements adhere to the principles of the accrual method of accounting.

Under this accrual method, revenue is recognized when it is earned, rather than when it is received. In contrast, the tax credits that have been claimed were done so in accordance with the tax deduction certificates provided to the appellant by their customers. These certificates are typically issued based on the tax withheld at the source and may not necessarily align perfectly with the accrual-based revenue recognition in the financial statements.

In simpler terms, the timing of when revenue is recognized for accounting purposes and when tax credits are claimed may differ due to the distinct criteria governing these processes. This discrepancy does not imply any wrongdoing but rather reflects the inherent variations in accounting and taxation methodologies.

The background of aforesaid decision of SCP is that the respondent company is based in Netherlands, which had no business presence in Pakistan. Expenditure Incurred Wholly and Exclusively for the Purpose of Business:

In the realm of taxation, the concept of "expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business" stands as a fundamental principle that guides the determination of allowable deductions for businesses. This foundational concept is integral to understanding and applying tax laws, ensuring a fair and accurate representation of a company's financial standing. Here, we delve into the key aspects of this principle and its significance in the context of business taxation.

1. **Definition and Significance:**
   The phrase "wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business" encapsulates the notion that allowable business expenses must be directly related to the generation of income. To qualify for deduction, an expense must be incurred with the sole intention of conducting and promoting the business operations.

2. **Necessity and Business Connection:**
   For an expense to meet the criterion of being wholly and exclusively for business purposes, it should be a necessary and integral part of the business operations. The connection between the expenditure and the business must be genuine, with a clear link between the cost incurred and the revenue-generating activities.

3. **Ordinary and Necessary Expenses:**
   Generally, ordinary and necessary business expenses fall within the ambit of being wholly and exclusively incurred for business purposes. These can include costs related to production, marketing, distribution, employee wages, rent, utilities, and other day-to-day operational expenses.

4. **Exclusions and Personal Elements:**
   Personal or non-business-related elements within an expense can render it non-deductible. When an expenditure serves a dual purpose, with both personal and business elements, the tax authorities may scrutinize the allocation of costs to ensure that the claimed deduction is proportionate to the business-related component.

5. **Documentation and Substantiation:**
   Proper documentation is crucial to substantiate that an expense meets the criteria of being wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business. Businesses are often required to maintain records, receipts, and other evidence that clearly demonstrate the business nature of the expenditure.

2. **Sequence and Proceedings**: According to CP No.2447-L/2022, proceedings under Section 111 must conclude before action under Section 122 can commence. This ensures that the taxpayer has an opportunity to respond to allegations raised under Section 111(1) before a final opinion is formed by the Commissioner.

3. **Section 122(5) vs. Section 122(5A)**: Section 122(5) addresses undisclosed income or misstatements, while Section 122(5A) addresses non-payment or underpayment of tax. The case argues that premature use of Section 122(5A) before completing Section 111 proceedings violates due process.

4. **Legal Framework and Compliance**: After completing Section 111 proceedings, only Section 122(5) should be invoked, not Section 122(5A). This adherence ensures fair opportunity for the taxpayer to respond and upholds the integrity of tax assessment procedures.

This ensures that the taxpayer is fully aware of the allegations and has an opportunity to provide explanations, maintaining the principles of due process and fair trial.

Subject: Important Information on Penalties for Non-Issuance of Sales Tax Invoice and Delay in Sales Tax Registration

Dear [Client's Name],

I hope this email finds you well.

We would like to bring to your attention the penalties outlined in the Sales Tax Act concerning the non-issuance of sales tax invoices and delays in obtaining sales tax registration. Below are the relevant penalties you should be aware of:

**1. Failure to Issue a Sales Tax Invoice:**
- **Offence:** Any person who fails to issue an invoice when required under the Act.
- **Penalty:** Such person shall pay a penalty of five thousand rupees or three percent of the amount of the tax involved, whichever is higher.
- **Relevant Section:** Section 23

**2. Unauthorized Issuance of a Sales Tax Invoice:**
- **Offence:** Any person who unauthorizedly issues an invoice in which an amount of tax is specified.
- **Penalty:** Such person shall pay a penalty of ten thousand rupees or five percent of the amount of the tax involved, whichever is higher.
- **Relevant Sections:** Sections 3, 7, and 23

**3. Failure to Apply for Sales Tax Registration:**
- **Offence:** Any person who is required to apply for registration under the Act but fails to make an application for registration before making taxable supplies.
- **Penalty:** Such person shall pay a penalty of ten thousand rupees or five percent of the amount of tax involved, whichever is higher.
- **Further Penalty:** If the person fails to get registered within sixty days of the commencement of taxable activity, they shall, upon conviction by a Special Judge, be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine which may extend to an amount equal to the amount of tax involved, or with both.
- **Relevant Section:** Section 14

It is crucial to ensure compliance with these requirements to avoid the penalties mentioned above. Please review your current practices and take necessary actions to align with the provisions of the Sales Tax Act.

Should you have any questions or need further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Subject: Update on Sindh Board of Revenue's New Procedure for Collection and Payment of Tax on Distribution Services

Dear [Client's Name],

I hope this email finds you well.

I am writing to inform you about an important update from the Sindh Board of Revenue regarding the procedure for the collection and payment of tax on distribution services. Please find the key points outlined below:

**42M. Procedure for Collection and Payment of Tax on Distribution Services:**

1. **Applicability:**
   The provisions of this rule apply to persons providing or rendering distribution services under tariff heading 9845.0000.

2. **Registration:**
   Every person providing or rendering such services must register in terms of section 24 of the Act, as detailed in Chapter II of these rules.

3. **Value of Taxable Services:**
   The value of taxable services for distribution of goods is 8% of the gross margin of the distributor.
   - **Explanation:** The term “gross margin” includes trade margin, trade discount, trade offer, commission, rebate, or any other incentive received by distributors in relation to distribution services.

4. **Tax Rate:**
   The standard tax rate on these services is 15%.
   - **Note:** The tax rate for services related to the distribution of drugs registered under the Drugs Act, 1976, is reduced to 5% as per notification No. SRB-3-4/8/2013 dated 1st July 2013, amended by notification No. SRB-3-4/24/2024 dated 29th June 2024.

5. **Invoicing:**
   Every service provider must issue a serially-numbered invoice or bill of charges, electronically or otherwise, containing the particulars specified in sub-rule (1) of rule 29. A copy must be provided to the service recipient.

6. **Record Maintenance:**
   All service providers must maintain records as prescribed in section 26 of the Act and sub-rule (2A) of rule 29.

7. **Payment and Filing:**
   The tax for services provided in a tax period must be paid by the 15th of the month following the tax period. The tax return must be filed within three days from the due date for payment of tax, as prescribed in Chapter III of these rules.

Please ensure that your team is aware of these changes and complies with the new procedures. Should you have any questions or require further clarification, feel free to contact us.

The DCIR has incorrectly assessed FED of Rs 2,878,843 for the tax period 2008 and Rs 7,879,960 for the tax period 2009, totaling Rs 10,758,804. This assessment is based on a misunderstanding that the matter was remanded back by the Sindh High Court (SHC) through its order dated September 14, 2022. 

In reality, the appellant had filed a special federal excise reference application before the SHC against the consolidated order of the ATIR dated July 10, 2013. The SHC, in its order dated September 14, 2022, noted that the ATIR had already rectified/amended its earlier consolidated order on March 18, 2014, and had remanded the matter back to the department for de novo proceedings. Consequently, the appellant's purpose of filing the reference application was considered served, and the SHC dismissed the reference applications as infructuous.

There was no directive from the SHC for remand back proceedings, as erroneously claimed by the DCIR.

The DCIR has failed to acknowledge that the impugned order is invalid due to time limitations. Under section 14B(1) of the FED Act, an order reflecting the findings of an appellate authority must be passed within one year from the end of the financial year in which the appellate authority's order was served. The ATIR's order dated March 18, 2014, predates the insertion of section 14B(1) via the Finance Act, 2018. Legally, the order should have been issued by June 30, 2020. As the de novo proceedings were not concluded within this statutory period, the orders dated June 28, 2024, are time-barred and thus illegal.

The DCIR has incorrectly recovered FED for tax periods before the date of compulsory registration. The ATIR, in STA No. 204/IB/2021, determined that tax obligations under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, begin from the compulsory registration date and cannot be applied retroactively. Since the compulsory registration provisions under the FED Act mirror those of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, the company cannot be held liable for FED for periods before its compulsory registration date. Rule 3A(5) of the Federal Excise Rules, 2005, also states that compliance with FED Act provisions starts from the compulsory registration date.

This section includes any employer-paid or reimbursed expenditure unless it is specifically for office duties, with proper documentation. HR policies should avoid the term 'fuel allowance' and instead clarify that fuel is for official purposes via fuel cards. Fuel cards for general travel are taxable perquisites. Additionally, any allowance for short consumption beyond the entitled limit should be treated as taxable fuel allowance under Section 12(2)(c).

Regarding income tax, please note that under Section 235 of the Ordinance, advance tax is required to be collected on the amount of the electricity bill for commercial, industrial, or domestic consumers. The Finance Act of 2017 clarified that the term 'electricity bill' for the purpose of advance tax includes sales tax and all other incidental charges. However, incidental charges are generally minor and directly related to the supply of electricity. Since MUCT charges are neither included in the electricity tariff nor incidental to the supply of electricity, they should not be considered when collecting advance tax under Section 235 of the Ordinance.

It is pertinent to highlight here that recovery of taxes should be commence from the date of compulsory registration and cannot be applied retroactively. In the case STA No. 204/IB/2021, involving M/s Muhammad Shoaib C/o Shoaib Traders, challenges an order from the Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-I, RTO, Sargodha, regarding the appellant's sales tax liability for the tax periods from July 2017 to June 2018. The dispute centers around the timing and applicability of the appellant's sales tax obligations under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The appellant, M/s Muhammad Shoaib C/o Shoaib Traders, was compulsorily registered for sales tax purposes on February 19, 2020. The Commissioner Inland Revenue assessed a sales tax liability for the for periods from July 2017 to June 2018, which included months before the appellant's compulsory registration.

The taxpayer contended that their obligation to comply with sales tax provisions should commence from the date of compulsory registration. They referenced sub-rule (4) of rule 6 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, which states that the provisions of the Act and Rules apply from the date of registration. The appellant argued that tax liability should not be retroactively applied to periods before their official registration date. The Commissioner Inland Revenue assessed the tax liability based on taxable supplies made by the appellant prior to their registration, asserting that the appellant was responsible for sales tax on these supplies even before their formal registration under the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

The ATIR, Islamabad in STA No. 204/IB/2021 vide order dated March 15, 2022, examined the legal provisions and the taxpayer's arguments. The Tribunal found that the liability to comply with the Sales Tax Act and Rules indeed begins from the date of compulsory registration, not retroactively. The Tribunal approved the taxpayer’s view that no recovery of taxes should be made for tax periods before the date of compulsory registration, as the legal obligation to comply with the Sales Tax Act only arises from that date.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal on legal grounds, establishing that the taxpayer, should not be held liable for sales tax periods prior to its compulsory registration. This decision reinforces the principle that tax obligations under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, commence from the date of compulsory registration and cannot be applied retroactively.

Keeping in view of the above, since client's sales tax registration was canceled by the Central Registration Office w.e.f. July 09, 2008, following the order from the Customs, Excise, and Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) dated May 19, 2007. As a result, our client was not obliged comply with sales tax obligations associated with registered persons for tax periods after cancellation of registration. This principle was reinforced by the ATIR in the case of M/s Muhammad Shoaib C/o Shoaib Traders, where the Tribunal ruled that tax obligations under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, start from the date of compulsory registration. Therefore, given that our client’s STRN was canceled, and no compulsory registration was made through, no tax recovery is possible for the tax periods following the cancellation of registration.

No Jurisdiction of the Federal Government to Charge FED on or after July 1, 2011

Notwithstanding with sales tax registration status, without prejudice to above, we would like to inform your good office that the right of levying taxes on ‘services’ has become the provincial matter after 18th Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan and that any kind of tax / duty levied by the Federation on ‘service’ is unlawful. Thus, after the promulgation of the provincial sales tax laws on services, FE Act, 2005 in so far as they relate to providing of ‘services’ (except in the case of shipping agents, freight forwarders) ultra-vires the Constitution of Pakistan w.e.f. July 1, 2011.

In the case reported as 2017 PTD 1 the SHC (on page 65) has held that “on account of the 18th Amendment to the Constitution (and by reason of the addition of the “exception” to entry No. 49 of the Federal Legislative List), the said provisions are declared to be ultra vires the Constitution, with effect from 01.07.2011 in relation to the Province of Sindh.”

The above judgement has been relied upon by the SHC in another judgement of the SHC in the case of Telecommunication companies in C.P. No. D-4778 to 4780 of 2021 dated October 8, 2021, in relation to entry No. 6A in Table II of First Schedule to Federal Excise Act, 2005 which was introduced vide Finance Act, 2021. The said entry imposes FED at the rate of 75 paisa per call if it exceeds five minutes. The SHC at paragraph 32 of the order has held that “the imposition of federal excise duty on services in the area of province of Sindh after 01.07.2011 having been declared to be unconstitutional in the aforesaid judgment to which we find no reason to disagree and likewise 6A would not withstand the exclusion made in Entry 49 to Federal Legislative List.”

Since Federal Excise Act, 2005 has been held to be ultra vires the Constitution with reference to taxable services within the Provincial domain with effect from July 1, 2011, the show cause notice dated March 7, 2012, issued to our client (i.e., after July 1, 2011) is void ab-initio as it transgresses and directly encroaches the Provincial jurisdiction with regards to sales tax on services.

Similarly, the Chairman Bench of the ATIR in the case of PAKSAT International (Private) Limited vide order in STA No. 182/KB/2015 dated February 16, 2016 has held that after the promulgation of SSTSA with effect from July 1, 2011, the taxation officer of FBR does not have the jurisdiction to initiate any proceeding to recover tax on services (which are presently covered by the provincial laws) even in respect of periods prior to promulgation of the SSTSA. It is, therefore, contended that continuation of orders passed by the taxation officer of FBR is without jurisdiction and is liable to be annulled ab-initio. It has been held that:

“13. We are of the view that at the strength of 18th amendment, the provisions of section 83(6) of SST Act, SRB has ousted the jurisdiction of FBR for collecting taxes for all prior years except where proceedings have already been initiated before promulgation of SSTSA. Sub-section (6) of section 83 of SSTSA is reproduced below for ready reference:

"(6) Any proceeding relating to an assessment in respect of any financial year ending prior to the date notified under sub-section (3) of section 1 will be initiated after the date notified under sub-section (3) of section 1 will be initiated and conducted in accordance with procedure specified in this Act.”


14. After implementation of the relevant laws by the provinces to tax services, the officer of the FBR cannot initiate any proceeding to recover tax on services (which are presently covered by the provincial laws) in respect of past years. In the instant case, it is evident that the proceeding initiated by the Taxation Officer to recover tax on services- relating to prior years lacks proper jurisdiction and is the impugned order is therefore annulled being passed by the taxation officer without having jurisdiction.” 
(emphasis is our)


The above proceedings were ab-initio invalid and unlawful. This is because the proceedings were initiated after July 1, 2011, i.e., the effective date of the promulgation of Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011 [SSTA] provided in section 1(3) read with section 83(6) of SSTSA. The action of the taxation officer is thus in transgression of the lawful jurisdiction and void ab-initio.
